name: PIC18F45K50-I_PT
title: PIC18(L)F2X/45K50 8-bit PIC18 microcontrollers with full-speed USB 2.0, 48 MHz, 16 or 32 Kbytes Flash, 28/40/44 pins
summary: An 8-bit PIC18 family with a crystal-less full-speed and low-speed USB 2.0 device module, its own transceiver and 3.3 V USB regulator, and a 16 MHz internal oscillator that tunes itself to the USB host or a 32.768 kHz crystal. It runs at up to 48 MHz (12 MIPS) with 16 or 32 Kbytes of Flash, 2048 bytes of SRAM (1 Kbyte of it shared with USB) and 256 bytes of data EEPROM, and carries a 10-bit A/D converter, two comparators, a 5-bit DAC, a fixed voltage reference, the CTMU for capacitive touch, ECCP and CCP, MSSP (SPI/I2C), an EUSART and an SR latch. F devices run from 2.3 V to 5.5 V on an internal core regulator; LF devices from 1.8 V to 3.6 V. PIC18F45K50-I/PT is the 32 Kbyte F device in the 44-pin TQFP for -40 °C to +85 °C.
key_figures: 8-bit PIC18, DC to 48 MHz (12 MIPS), 8 x 8 single-cycle hardware multiplier, 31-level return stack
32 Kbytes Flash (16384 single-word instructions), 2048 bytes SRAM, 256 bytes data EEPROM
F devices 2.3 V to 5.5 V; LF devices 1.8 V to 3.6 V
V2.0, full speed 12 Mb/s and low speed 1.5 Mb/s, up to 32 endpoints (16 bidirectional), 1 Kbyte dual-access RAM, on-chip transceiver
HFINTOSC 16 MHz, factory calibrated to ± 1%, self-tune to ± 0.20% max from USB or secondary oscillator; INTRC 31 kHz
3x (from 16 MHz) or 4x (from 8 MHz to 12 MHz) to reach 48 MHz
Sleep 20 nA typ; Watchdog Timer 300 nA typ; Timer1 oscillator 800 nA at 32 kHz
up to 33 I/O plus 3 input-only pins, 25 mA sink/source
10-bit A/D, up to 25 channels; two comparators; 5-bit DAC; FVR 1.024 V, 2.048 V, 4.096 V
Flash 10,000 erase/write cycles minimum, 20-year data retention

notes: (1) CCP2 can be moved to its alternate pin by a Configuration bit.

(3) These pins work only when ICPRT = 1; otherwise they are disabled.
(4) Location on the 40/44-pin parts (PIC18(L)F45K50); the 28-pin parts (PIC18(L)F2XK50) do not have this function on this pin.
(5) Location on the 28-pin parts (PIC18(L)F2XK50); the 40/44-pin parts (PIC18(L)F45K50) do not have this function on this pin.
(6) SDO can be moved to its alternate pin by Configuration bits.
(7) RE3 is a digital input only; it has no output driver.

circuits.title: Recommended minimum connections
circuits.description: The connections every design needs: a 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor across each VDD/VSS pair (two pairs on the 44-pin TQFP), a reset network on MCLR, and a low-ESR ceramic capacitor from VUSB3V3 to ground to keep the internal USB regulator stable on F devices. R1 pulls MCLR up, C1 filters it, and R2 sits between the network and the pin.

parts.note: 20 V ceramic, at VDD pin 7 / VSS pin 6
20 V ceramic, at VDD pin 28 / VSS pin 29
VUSB3V3 regulator capacitor; the electrical specifications set its value

notes: One 0.1 µF capacitor goes on each VDD/VSS pair the package has; the 44-pin TQFP has two pairs.
On LF devices the regulator is off and VUSB3V3 is tied to a supply held at the VDD level instead of the capacitor.

circuits.title: MCLR connections with a jumper for programming
circuits.description: MCLR pull-up R1 and series resistor R2, with the filter capacitor C1 joined through a jumper so it can be lifted off the pin while a programmer or debugger drives MCLR, and refitted for normal running. R2 limits current from C1 into the pin if the pin breaks down under ESD or EOS. All parts within 6 mm (0.25 inch) of the pin.

parts.note: 10 kΩ is the starting value; MCLR VIH and VIL must still be met
MCLR VIH and VIL must still be met

circuits.title: External clock (EC) mode connections
circuits.description: A logic-level clock from an outside system drives OSC1/CLKIN; OSC2 is then free as general-purpose I/O (or gives FOSC/4 in the CLKO variants). No start-up timer runs in EC mode.

circuits.title: Quartz crystal operation (LP, XT or HS mode)
circuits.description: A quartz crystal between OSC1 and OSC2 with a load capacitor from each side to ground; the inverting amplifier and its feedback resistor RF (typically 2 MΩ to 10 MΩ, set by the oscillator mode) are inside the part. RS, in series at OSC2, may be needed for crystals with a low drive level.

parts.note: fitted only when the crystal's drive level needs it

notes: Crystal characteristics differ by type, package and vendor; oscillator behaviour is to be checked over the VDD and temperature range of the design.

circuits.title: Ceramic resonator operation (XT or HS mode)
circuits.description: A ceramic resonator between OSC1 and OSC2 with load capacitors to ground. A parallel feedback resistor RP across the resonator may be needed for it to run properly, and a series resistor RS at OSC2 for resonators with a low drive level; the internal feedback resistor RF is typically 2 MΩ to 10 MΩ depending on mode.

parts.note: fitted only when the resonator needs it
fitted only when the resonator's drive level needs it

circuits.title: External RC oscillator modes
circuits.description: REXT from VDD and CEXT to VSS meet at OSC1/CLKIN and set the oscillator frequency, which also depends on VDD, temperature, the input threshold, part tolerances and package capacitance. In RC mode OSC2/CLKO gives FOSC/4; in RCIO mode OSC2 is general-purpose I/O.

circuits.title: External power-on reset circuit for a slow VDD rise
circuits.description: Needed only when VDD ramps up too slowly for the internal POR. R charges C from VDD, and the capacitor node drives MCLR through R1; diode D, anode at the capacitor and cathode at VDD, empties C quickly when VDD falls. R1 limits the current from C into MCLR/VPP if the pin breaks down under ESD or EOS.

parts.note: keeps the drop across R within the electrical specification

circuits.title: Standard half-bridge (push-pull) circuit
circuits.description: ECCP1 in half-bridge mode drives two N-channel MOSFETs stacked between the positive end of an upper supply and ground, each through its own FET driver: P1A switches the upper FET, P1B the lower one with the complementary signal. Two supplies in series make a centre point; the load hangs between the FETs' junction and that centre point, so it sees either supply in turn. The programmable dead-band delay keeps both FETs from conducting together.

circuits.title: Half-bridge output driving a full-bridge circuit
circuits.description: ECCP1 in half-bridge mode runs a four-MOSFET H-bridge between V+ and ground with only two signals. P1A drives the upper-left and lower-right FETs through their drivers; the complementary P1B drives the lower-left and upper-right FETs. The load sits across the two bridge mid-points, so current reverses through it each half of the PWM cycle; the dead-band delay guards against shoot-through in each leg.

circuits.title: Full-bridge application
circuits.description: ECCP1 in full-bridge mode drives an H-bridge of four N-channel MOSFETs between V+ and V-, one driver per FET: P1A to upper-left QA, P1B to lower-left QB, P1C to upper-right QC and P1D to lower-right QD. The load spans the two bridge mid-points. In forward mode QA is held on while QD is modulated; in reverse mode QC is held on while QB is modulated.

circuits.title: SPI master and multiple slave connection
circuits.description: One SPI master shares its clock and data lines with three slaves and gives each slave its own select line from a general-purpose I/O pin. SCLK and master SDO go to every slave's SCLK and SDI; the slaves' SDO outputs join on the master's SDI, and only the selected slave drives it. The PIC18F45K50 sits in the first slave position through its MSSP pins.
notes: SCK and SDI share pins with SCL and SDA on RB1 and RB0; SDO is on RC7.

circuits.title: SPI master/slave connection
circuits.description: Two processors with MSSP ports joined as SPI master and slave. The master (SSPxM<3:0> = 00xx or 1010) drives SCK and sends on SDO into the slave's SDI; the slave (SSPxM<3:0> = 010x) answers on its SDO into the master's SDI, each byte swapping the two shift registers. A general-purpose I/O pin of the master can drive the slave's SS input; the select line is optional. The PIC18F45K50 is the slave.
notes: The slave select line is optional.

circuits.title: SPI daisy-chain connection
circuits.description: Three SPI slaves chained behind one master: the master's SDO feeds the first slave's SDI, each slave's SDO feeds the next slave's SDI, and the last slave's SDO returns to the master's SDI. SCLK and one select line from a general-purpose I/O pin go to all three slaves. The PIC18F45K50 is the first slave; with BOEN set it accepts new bytes for the chain without reading the previous ones.

circuits.title: I2C master/slave connection
circuits.description: The PIC18F45K50 as I2C master joined to a slave on the two open-drain bus lines. SCL and SDA each have a pull-up resistor to VDD, so a released line reads 1 and either device can pull it to 0.

circuits.title: CTMU current source calibration circuit
circuits.description: A precision resistor RCAL from an unused analog input to ground. With the CTMU current source switched onto that channel, the A/D reads the voltage across RCAL and the current is V / RCAL.

parts.note: for the 0.55 µA range at a 3.3 V reference (420 kΩ for 5.5 µA, 42 kΩ for 55 µA); 0.1% tolerance or better

notes: Any unused analog channel serves; the sample calibration routine uses AN2.

circuits.title: Typical connections for CTMU time measurement
circuits.description: Two edge signals on CTED1 and CTED2 start and stop the CTMU current source, which charges the A/D converter's sample capacitor through the selected channel; the voltage converted is proportional to the time between the edges. A resistor RPR runs from the ANx pin to ground.
notes: ANx can be any analog channel.

circuits.title: Typical connections for CTMU pulse delay generation
circuits.description: An edge on CTED1 starts the CTMU current source charging CPULSE on the C12IN1- pin, the inverting input of comparator 2; when the capacitor reaches the CVREF trip point the comparator ends the pulse output on CTPLS, so CPULSE sets the pulse width.

circuits.title: DAC voltage reference output buffer
circuits.description: The DAC voltage comes out on DACOUT through the ladder's own output impedance, so it can supply almost no current. A capacitor to ground on DACOUT and an op amp wired as a voltage follower give a low-impedance copy of the DAC level for outside use.
notes: DACOE = 1 puts the DAC on DACOUT (RA2).

circuits.title: USB full-speed connection with external pull-up
circuits.description: Full-speed attach using the internal 3.3 V regulator and an external pull-up. A 1.5 kΩ resistor from VUSB3V3 to D+ signals a full-speed device; VUSB3V3 has its bypass capacitor to ground, and D+ and D- go straight to the host or hub.
notes: With an external pull-up the internal pull-ups are turned off (UPUEN = 0).

circuits.title: USB bus power only
circuits.description: The whole device runs from VBUS. VBUS feeds VDD with a bulk capacitor to ground, and VUSB3V3 has its own capacitor to VSS. The capacitance across VBUS must stay at 10 µF or less for the USB inrush limit.
notes: C1 is polarised, positive to VBUS.

circuits.title: USB self power only
circuits.description: The device runs from its own supply VSELF and takes almost nothing from USB. VSELF feeds VDD with a bulk capacitor to ground, and VUSB3V3 has its own capacitor to VSS. The module and pull-up stay off until the host drives VBUS high.
notes: C1 is polarised, positive to VSELF.

circuits.title: USB dual power with self-power dominance
circuits.description: VDD comes from the local supply VSELF (about 5 V) through a diode while it is present; a PNP transistor from VBUS (about 5 V) takes over when it is not. The transistor's base is tied through a 100 kΩ resistor to VSELF, which holds it off, and a second resistor from VSELF to ground pulls the base low so the transistor conducts when VSELF is absent. A bulk capacitor holds VDD, and VUSB3V3 has its own capacitor to VSS.
notes: C1 is polarised, positive to VDD.
A device powered from USB may draw at most 100 mA (low power) or 500 mA (high power).

operation.text: USB V2.0 device module with its own transceiver, full speed at 12 Mb/s and low speed at 1.5 Mb/s, needing no crystal. It handles control, interrupt, isochronous and bulk transfers on up to 32 endpoints (16 bidirectional) and has 1 Kbyte of RAM that both the CPU and USB engine can reach.

PLL multipliers of 3x and 4x; an external clock input in two modes, to 48 MHz or 12 MIPS; a 31 kHz internal oscillator; an internal oscillator from 31 kHz to 16 MHz, calibrated at the factory to ± 1% and able to tune itself to ± 0.20% max against USB or the secondary oscillator; a 32 kHz secondary oscillator on Timer1; and a fail-safe clock monitor that lets the part shut down safely if any clock stops.

Up to 33 I/O pins plus 3 that are input only, each sinking or sourcing 25 mA, with three external interrupts, 11 interrupt-on-change pins, nine weak pull-ups and programmable slew rate. SR latch; ECCP with one, two or four PWM outputs, selectable polarity, programmable dead time, auto-shutdown and auto-restart and pulse steering; a CCP; an MSSP for 3-wire SPI (all four modes) and I2C master and slave; and an EUSART with RS-485, RS-232 and LIN/J2602 support, wake-up on a start bit and auto-baud.

Two comparators with input multiplexing. A 10-bit A/D converter with up to 25 input channels, automatic acquisition and conversion during Sleep. A DAC block holding the fixed voltage reference (1.024 V, 2.048 V and 4.096 V) and a 5-bit rail-to-rail resistive DAC with selectable positive and negative references. A high/low-voltage detector, and the CTMU, which supports capacitive touch screens and switches.

operation.topic: Features: low power and special functions
operation.text: Typical currents: Sleep 20 nA, Watchdog Timer 300 nA, Timer1 oscillator 800 nA at 32 kHz; peripherals can be disabled one by one. Run (CPU, peripherals and SRAM on), Idle (CPU off) and Sleep (CPU and peripherals off, SRAM kept). Two interrupt priority levels, self-programming under software control, an 8 x 8 single-cycle multiplier, an extended watchdog with a period from 4 ms to 131 s, single-supply ICSP and in-circuit debug with three breakpoints over two pins, and an optional dedicated ICD/ICSP port on the 44-pin TQFP. Flash is rated for 10,000 erase/write cycles minimum with 20-year retention. F devices run from 2.3 V to 5.5 V and LF devices from 1.8 V to 3.6 V.

The family is PIC18(L)F45K50, PIC18(L)F25K50 and PIC18(L)F24K50, in 28-pin and 40/44-pin packages. They differ in Flash size, number of A/D channels, I/O ports, and input voltage range with power consumption; everything else is the same. The 'L' parts are the LF (1.8 V to 3.6 V) devices.

Running from Timer1 or the internal oscillator block can cut execution power by up to 90%; the Idle modes, CPU stopped and peripherals running, go down to about 4% of normal. Peripheral Module Disable bits remove power from unused modules in Run and Idle, mode changes are made by software on the fly, and Timer1 and the Watchdog Timer draw very little.
A full USB 2.0 communications module with built-in transceiver handles low-speed and full-speed communication for every supported transfer type; the part carries its own 3.3 V regulator for USB.

Ten oscillator options: four crystal modes for crystals or ceramic resonators; six external clock modes using either two pins (input plus a divide-by-four clock output) or one pin (the second pin becomes I/O); two external RC modes with the same pin choices; and the internal block of a 16 MHz HFINTOSC and a 31 kHz INTRC giving eight software-selected frequencies from 31 kHz to 16 MHz, leaving both oscillator pins free as I/O. The 3x and 4x PLLs work with external and internal sources for clocks up to 48 MHz, so 31 kHz to 48 MHz is possible with no external crystal. Active clock tuning trims the internal oscillator to the USB host or a 32.768 kHz secondary oscillator, which lets full-speed USB meet its specification without a crystal. The fail-safe clock monitor watches the main clock against the INTRC and moves to the internal block on a failure, and two-speed start-up runs from the internal oscillator after POR or wake-up until the primary source is ready.

Flash cells for program memory last up to 10K erase/write cycles and data EEPROM cells up to 100K; retention without refresh is estimated at over 40 years. The part can write its own program memory, so a bootloader in the protected boot block at the top of memory can update the application in the field. An optional extended instruction set adds eight instructions and an indexed addressing mode suited to re-entrant code from high-level languages such as C; it is enabled by a configuration bit. The ECCP gives 1, 2 or 4 PWM outputs for half- and full-bridge drivers with auto-shutdown, auto-restart and output steering. The EUSART does RS-232 and LIN with auto-baud and a 16-bit baud rate generator, and works from the internal oscillator without a crystal. The 10-bit A/D has programmable acquisition time so a conversion can start without waiting out a sampling period. The TQFP option of dedicated ICD/ICSP pins frees the multiplexed pins for the application. The CTMU measures time differences between pulse sources and with other on-chip analog modules measures capacitance or changes in it; it also generates pulses independent of the system clock. The SR latch has several set and reset inputs and separate outputs.

Always connected: every VDD and VSS pin, MCLR and VUSB3V3. Connected when used: PGC/PGD for ICSP and debugging, OSC1/OSC2 when an external oscillator runs. VREF+ and VREF- are needed only when the analog modules use an external reference.

Each VDD/VSS pair takes a decoupling capacitor: 0.1 µF (100 nF), 10-20 V, low ESR, ceramic, with self-resonance at 200 MHz or above. Place it as close to the pins as possible, on the same side of the board as the part; if it must go on another layer through a via, keep the trace from pin to capacitor at 6 mm (0.25 inch) or less. Against noise of tens of MHz and up, add a second ceramic of 0.01 µF to 0.001 µF beside each one (for example 0.1 µF with 0.001 µF). Route supply and return from the power source to the capacitors first, then on to the pins, with short capacitor-to-pin traces to keep inductance low.

Where supply traces run longer than six inches, a local tank capacitor is suggested, sized from the trace resistance and the peak current so the voltage sag at the part stays acceptable; typical values are 4.7 µF to 47 µF.

MCLR serves both as device reset and as the programming and debug pin. Where programming and debugging are not needed, tying it straight to VDD may be enough, and extra parts can make the part more immune to spurious resets from supply sags. Programmers and debuggers drive MCLR, so the resistance and capacitance added must not spoil the VIH/VIL levels or the fast edges: R1 and C1 are chosen for the design, and C1 may be isolated with a jumper during programming. Keep every MCLR component within 6 mm (0.25 inch) of the pin.

The on-chip regulator pin always connects either to a supply or to an external capacitor. On F devices the regulator is permanently on and VUSB3V3 needs a low-ESR capacitor, ceramic recommended, to ground; it must not be tied to VDD, and the trace should stay under 6 mm (0.25 inch). On LF devices (PIC18LF2X/45K50) the regulator is permanently off, VUSB3V3 is tied to a source held at VDD, and VDD must meet the 'regulator disabled' limits of parameter D001.

Ceramic capacitors suit the internal regulator, provided the capacitance holds over the operating range. X5R and X7R start at ±10% to ±20% and are about ±15% over temperature; Y5V starts at -20%/+80% and can move +22%/-82% with temperature, so a nominal 10 µF Y5V may fall short of the regulator's stability and transient needs and is not recommended for wide-temperature designs. DC bias also lowers the capacitance of large ceramics markedly; picking a rating well above the working voltage helps, for example a 16 V part for the 3.3 V on VUSB3V3.

Keep the traces from the ICSP connector to PGC and PGD short. If the connector may see ESD, a series resistor of a few tens of ohms, no more than 100 Ω, is recommended. Pull-ups, series diodes and capacitors on PGC and PGD disturb programmer and debugger traffic; remove them while programming, or meet the capacitive loading and VIH/VIL limits of the Flash programming specification. For emulation the configured PGCx/PGDx channel must match the pins wired to the tool.

Place the oscillator circuit on the same side as the part, within 12 mm (0.5 inch) of its pins, with the load capacitors next to the crystal. Surround it with a grounded copper pour tied straight to the MCU ground, with no signal or power traces inside the pour and, on a two-sided board, none on the far side under the crystal. Fine-pitch packages may not allow a full guard ring; the broken pieces can be tied to a mirrored ground layer, and every guard returns to ground. Neighbouring port pins and signals near the oscillator should carry no high frequencies or fast edges.
Make unused pins outputs driven low, or tie each to VSS through 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ and drive the output low.

Clock sources: external oscillators, quartz crystals, ceramic resonators and RC circuits, plus three internal oscillators with software-selected speeds. Extras: software selection between external and internal sources, two-speed start-up, the fail-safe clock monitor (FSCM) for LP, XT, HS, EC and RC sources, and the oscillator start-up timer (OST) for crystals. The primary clock is one of RC, LP, XT, INTOSC, HS or EC, chosen by FOSC<3:0> in CONFIG1H; FOSC<3:0> also tunes the HS and EC circuits for power against speed and lets RA6 be I/O or CLKO (FOSC/4) in RC, EC and INTOSC modes. PCLKEN, PRISD, CFGPLLEN, PLLEN, IRCF<2:0> and INTSRC further shape the primary clock. HFINTOSC and INTRC are factory calibrated.

operation.topic: Oscillator control and system clock select
operation.text: OSCCON, OSCCON2 and OSCTUNE hold system clock select (SCS), primary oscillator shutdown (PRISD), secondary oscillator enable (SOSCGO), the PLL enable (PLLEN), frequency selection (IRCF, INTSRC), status (OSTS, HFIOFS, LFIOFS, SOSCRUN, PLLRDY) and IDLEN. SCS<1:0> picks the primary clock set by FOSC<3:0> (00), the secondary oscillator, the 32.768 kHz source shared with Timer1 and Timer3 (01), or the internal oscillator block (1x). A write switches after a short transition; every Reset clears SCS to the primary clock. Automatic switches by two-speed start-up or the FSCM do not change SCS; SOSCRUN, LFIOFS, HFIOFS and OSTS show which source is running.

IRCF<2:0> select INTRC (31.25 kHz), HFINTOSC (16 MHz) or a postscaler output from 31.25 kHz to 16 MHz, and a change takes effect at once when the internal block clocks the part. After any Reset the output is 1 MHz. At 31.25 kHz (IRCF = 000) INTSRC chooses between INTRC and a 31.25 kHz clock divided from HFINTOSC, which can be trimmed with TUN<6:0> while keeping the power of a slow clock. The WDT and FSCM always run from INTRC whatever INTSRC says. IDLEN decides whether SLEEP enters Sleep or an Idle mode.

In LP, XT and HS modes the OST counts 1024 oscillations on OSC1 after a POR (once the PWRT, if used, has run out) and after wake-up from Sleep; the program counter holds still meanwhile. Switching between sources also waits for the new clock to settle.

An external logic-level clock drives OSC1 and OSC2 is free for I/O. EC has three power levels set by FOSC<3:0>: ECL below 4 MHz, ECM from 4 MHz to 16 MHz and ECH above 16 MHz. The OST is off in EC mode, so there is no delay after POR or wake-up. The design is fully static: stopping the clock halts the part with all data kept, and restarting it carries on as if no time had passed.

A crystal or ceramic resonator on OSC1/OSC2 with the inverter-amplifier gain set by mode. LP has the lowest gain and current, for low-drive resonators such as tuning-fork crystals. XT is the middle gain and current, for medium drive. HS has a medium-power option for 4 MHz to 16 MHz and a high-power option, the highest gain, for above 16 MHz, for resonators needing high drive. The internal feedback resistor RF is typically 2 MΩ to 10 MΩ depending on mode.

RC mode puts an RC network on OSC1 and gives the RC frequency divided by 4 on OSC2/CLKO for outside use; RCIO mode makes OSC2 general-purpose I/O. Recommended values: 10 kΩ ≤ REXT ≤ 100 kΩ, CEXT > 20 pF. The frequency depends on VDD, REXT, CEXT, temperature, input threshold, component tolerance and package capacitance, so it suits designs where accuracy does not matter.

HFINTOSC runs at 16 MHz, factory calibrated and adjustable in software through OSCTUNE. INTRC runs at 31.25 kHz, factory calibrated, not adjustable and built to hold steady over voltage and temperature. Two FOSC<3:0> settings make the internal block the primary oscillator: in one OSC2/CLKO/RA6 is I/O (RA6), in the other it outputs FOSC/4 (CLKO); in both OSC1 is I/O.

INTRC feeds the primary or INTOSC clock and also always clocks the Power-up Timer, Watchdog Timer and Fail-Safe Clock Monitor. HFINTOSC drives a divider giving 16 MHz down to 31.25 kHz; IRCF<2:0> and INTSRC pick one of 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 (Reset default) MHz, 500 kHz, 250 kHz or 31 kHz.

operation.topic: Internal oscillator drift and manual tuning
operation.text: HFINTOSC is calibrated at 16 MHz but drifts with VDD and temperature. It can be tuned automatically by the active clock tuning module from USB or the secondary oscillator, or by hand with TUN<6:0>, which does not touch INTRC. Three ways to decide a manual trim: with the EUSART, framing errors mean the clock is fast (lower OSCTUNE) and data errors mean it is slow (raise it); with two timers, one on the peripheral clock and one on a reference such as the Timer1 oscillator, a count larger than expected means the oscillator is fast; with a CCP in capture mode timing an external event of known period, such as the mains frequency, a measured interval much longer than expected means fast and much shorter means slow.

The PLL lets a lower-frequency oscillator, or the internal oscillator, clock the part at up to its full rate, which can help with EMI from fast crystals. It works with any external mode on OSC1/OSC2 except the medium- and low-power FOSC selections, and is enabled by CFGPLLEN/PLLSEL in CONFIG1L or by PLLEN/SPLLMULT in OSCCON2 and OSCTUNE. 4x takes 8 MHz to 12 MHz up to 32 MHz to 48 MHz; 3x takes 16 MHz to 48 MHz. With HFINTOSC, set IRCF to 16 MHz for 3x and to 8 MHz for 4x.

In PRI_IDLE the primary oscillator keeps running; in every other power-managed mode the OSC1 oscillator stops. In SEC_RUN and SEC_IDLE the secondary oscillator clocks the part, and it may run in any mode to clock Timer1 or Timer3. In INTOSC_RUN and INTOSC_IDLE the internal block clocks the part; the 31.25 kHz INTRC can clock it directly and can stay on for the WDT, FSCM and two-speed start-up in any mode; HFINTOSC is off when INTRC supplies the clock directly. In Sleep every clock stops and only leakage remains; anything left running in Sleep adds current (the WDT needs INTRC; slave SSP and INTn work without a clock).

Two timers keep the part in reset until the supply and primary clock are stable, so most designs need no external reset parts. The PWRT gives a fixed delay at power-up when PWRTEN is cleared. The OST counts 1024 oscillator cycles in LP, XT and HS modes. With the PLL on in an external mode, the part runs from the base oscillator for 2 ms after the OST so the PLL can lock. After POR there is also a delay TCSD before instructions run, concurrent with the others and possibly the only one in EC, RC or INTOSC modes. With HFINTOSC as the primary clock, HFOFST in CONFIG3H chooses whether the system clock waits for HFINTOSC to be stable (cleared) or starts at once (set); HFIOFS shows when it is stable.

SCS<1:0> switch the system clock between sources, with glitch-free circuitry and a short pause. The sequence: after SCS changes the old clock runs until the new one is ready; two rising edges of the old clock after the ready signal, the system clock is held low from the next old-clock falling edge; after two more rising edges of the new clock it is released on the next falling edge, and the switch is done. If the new source is not running there is a start-up delay first; switching between two HFINTOSC-derived frequencies has none. OSTS, HFIOFR and LFIOFS show the current oscillator status. OSTS tells whether the system clock comes from the external source set by FOSC<3:0> or from the internal one, and in LP, XT and HS modes that the OST has run out.

Two-speed start-up removes the crystal start time from the time awake: after a POR (and PWRT, if on) or wake-up from Sleep, code runs at once from the internal oscillator at the IRCF frequency while the OST counts 1024 cycles; when it finishes OSTS sets and execution moves to the external oscillator. It needs IESO set in CONFIG1H, SCS<1:0> = 00 and FOSC set for LP, XT or HS. A SLEEP instruction during the start-up aborts it and leaves OSTS clear. OSTS = 0 means the part still runs from the internal oscillator.

The FSCM, enabled by FCMEN in CONFIG1H, covers LP, XT, HS, EC, RC and RCIO. A latch is set by each falling edge of the external clock and cleared by each rising edge of a sample clock, INTRC divided by 64 (about 488 Hz); a whole sample half-cycle without the primary clock going low is a failure. The part then switches to the internal clock chosen by IRCF<2:0> (which can be set up beforehand) and sets OSCFIF in PIR2, interrupting if OSCFIE in PIE2 is set; it never switches back to the failed clock by itself. Any Reset or toggling SCS1 clears the fail-safe condition and restarts the OST; the part runs from INTOSC until the OST times out and then returns to the external clock. OSCFIF can be cleared first. The FSCM is not active during oscillator start-up after Reset or Sleep, but it is active immediately in EC and RC modes, which have no OST. With FSCM in HS, XT or LP mode, IESO should also be set so the clock moves to the external oscillator when the OST ends.

The USB module needs 6 MHz for low speed or 48 MHz for full speed. The low-speed clock comes from the primary oscillator or the PLL: 48 MHz divided by 8 with LS48MHZ = 1, or 24 MHz divided by 4 with LS48MHZ = 0, while CPUDIV divides the CPU clock by 1, 2, 3 or 6.

The ACT module trims the 16 MHz internal oscillator continuously to ± 0.20% against an external reference, so a fast accurate crystal is not needed where a slower accurate clock exists, as in RTCC or full-speed USB designs. It is off after any Reset; ACTEN in ACTCON turns it on, after which it owns OSCTUNE and adjusts it every reference cycle; user writes to OSCTUNE are blocked though reads work, and after disabling the module wait three instructions before writing OSCTUNE. ACTSRC picks the reference: the full-speed USB module (ACT_clk) or the 32.768 kHz secondary clock (SOSC_clk). ACTLOCK sets once tuned and clears on loss of lock, Reset or disable. ACTORS sets when the needed OSCTUNE value is beyond the range at either end; the oscillator then keeps the last value, and ACTORS clears when tuning is back in range and locked. ACTUD suspends updates without disabling the module. ACTIF in PIR1 sets whenever ACTLOCK or ACTORS changes, whatever ACTIE (PIE1); it is cleared in software. The module does not run or interrupt in Sleep.

Seven operating modes in three groups: Run, Idle and Sleep. Run and Idle can use the primary, secondary or internal clock; Sleep uses none. IDLEN (OSCCON<7>) decides whether the CPU is clocked and SCS<1:0> (OSCCON<1:0>) choose the source. Loading OSCCON switches mode, immediately if the new clock is running; SLEEP enters Idle (IDLEN = 1, peripherals keep a clock) or Sleep (IDLEN = 0, all clocks stop). Often only SCS or IDLEN needs changing before SLEEP.

PRI_RUN, the default after Reset unless two-speed start-up is on, runs from the FOSC<3:0> oscillator. SEC_RUN (SCS = 01) runs from the secondary oscillator for low power with an accurate clock: the primary oscillator shuts down, SOSCRUN sets and OSTS clears; if SOSCGO and the SOSCEN bits are all clear, entry waits until SOSCGO is set and the oscillator is ready. Going back to PRI_RUN, the SOSC clocks the part until the primary clock is ready, then SOSCRUN clears and OSTS sets. RC_RUN (SCS1 = 1, SCS0 best cleared) runs from the INTOSC multiplexer with the primary clock off, the lowest-power Run mode on INTRC; it gains nothing when the primary clock is already the internal block and costs a switch delay. IRCF can change speed at any time. With IRCF and INTSRC all clear HFINTOSC stays off, HFIOFS stays clear and INTRC clocks the part; otherwise HFIOFS sets once the output is stable after TIOBST, clocks continuing meanwhile. Returning to PRI_RUN, INTOSC clocks the part until the primary clock is ready; INTRC keeps running if the WDT or FSCM is on.

Clearing IDLEN and executing SLEEP stops the selected oscillator and clears all clock status bits; no clock switch is needed. INTRC keeps running for the WDT and the SOSC keeps running if enabled. On a wake event (interrupt, Reset or WDT time-out) the part waits for the SCS-selected clock to be ready, or runs from the internal block if two-speed start-up or the FSCM is enabled; OSTS sets once the primary clock takes over, and IDLEN and SCS are unchanged.

On F devices an internal regulator supplies the core. VREGPM<1:0> in VREGCON trade Sleep current against wake-up time: 00 keeps the LDO in high-power mode always; 01 drops the LDO to low power during Sleep unless a peripheral needs high power; 10 turns the LDO off in Sleep with the ULP regulator active and the band gap forced on; 11 does the same without forcing the band gap. On LF devices the core runs directly from VDD, the regulator is bypassed and VREGCON does not exist.

With IDLEN = 1, SLEEP stops only the CPU while peripherals stay clocked from the SCS source; the clock status bits are untouched, INTRC runs for the WDT and the SOSC runs if enabled. Only an interrupt, WDT time-out or Reset ends Idle; the CPU starts after TCSD on the same clock as the Idle mode (RC_IDLE wakes into RC_RUN), and a WDT time-out wakes into the Run mode SCS selects. PRI_IDLE keeps the primary clock running for the fastest, most accurate restart and keeps OSTS set; enter it from PRI_RUN by setting IDLEN and executing SLEEP (from another Run mode, set IDLEN, clear SCS, then SLEEP). SEC_IDLE clocks the peripherals from the SOSC: from SEC_RUN set IDLEN and SLEEP, otherwise set IDLEN, set SCS = 01, then SLEEP; the primary oscillator stops, OSTS clears and SOSCRUN sets. The SOSC should already run and SOSCEN, T1CON<3> or T3CON<3> must be set at SLEEP, or the part enters PRI_IDLE or RC_IDLE instead. RC_IDLE clocks the peripherals from the HFINTOSC multiplexer: from RC_RUN set IDLEN and SLEEP, otherwise set IDLEN, set SCS1 (SCS0 best cleared), then SLEEP; IRCF may raise the frequency beforehand, the primary oscillator stops and OSTS clears; HFIOFS behaves as in RC_RUN.

An interrupt, a Reset or a WDT time-out ends Sleep or Idle. An interrupt needs its enable bit in INTCON or a PIE register; the instruction after SLEEP always runs, then the code branches to the vector if GIE/GIEH is set or carries on if not. A WDT time-out in Idle or Sleep wakes the part; in a Run mode it causes a WDT Reset. The WDT and postscaler clear on SLEEP, CLRWDT, loss of the selected clock with the FSCM on, or a change of IRCF while the internal block clocks the part. A Reset restarts code at address 0, with a delay that depends on the clocks before and after and the oscillator type. No OST runs when leaving PRI_IDLE (the clock never stopped) or when the primary source is not LP, XT, HS or HSPLL (RC, EC, INTOSC, INTOSCIO); a fixed TCSD delay always follows the wake event before execution resumes.

Peripherals still draw power in Idle. Setting a module's XXXMD bit in PMD0 or PMD1 removes all its clocks and the power to its control and status registers, so writes do nothing and reads are invalid; clearing the bit restores power and resets those registers to their defaults.

Resets: Power-on (POR); MCLR in normal operation and in power-managed modes; Watchdog Timer during execution; programmable Brown-out (BOR); the RESET instruction; stack full; stack underflow. RCON records them: its lower five bits flag which event happened, are mostly cleared only by the event and must be set again by software. RCON also holds IPEN (interrupt priority) and SBOREN (software BOR control). The reset logic combines the external reset (gated by MCLRE), the WDT, the POR detector, the BOR (BOREN), the stack pointer and the RESET instruction, with the OST (1024 cycles, 10-bit counter on OSC1) and PWRT (65.5 ms, 11-bit counter on the 32 µs INTRC) timing out the release; POR and BOR reset both counters.

Holding MCLR low resets the part; a noise filter ignores short pulses. A weak internal pull-up is on whenever the pin is MCLR. No internal reset, the WDT included, drives the pin low. The MCLRE configuration bit can turn MCLR off, leaving a digital input (RE3).

An on-chip POR pulse occurs when VDD rises past a threshold, so the part starts initialized. To use it, leave MCLR floating or tie it to VDD through a resistor; no external RC delay is needed, but VDD has a minimum rise rate, and a slower rise needs the external circuit. When reset ends, voltage, frequency and temperature must already be within limits, or the part must be held in reset until they are. POR clears the POR bit in RCON; no other reset changes it and no hardware sets it, so software sets it after each POR to catch later ones.

BORV<1:0> and BOREN<1:0> in CONFIG2L set the threshold and the mode. With BOR on (BOREN not 00), VDD below VBOR for longer than TBOR resets the part; shorter dips may or may not. The part stays in reset until VDD is above VBOR, then the PWRT, if enabled, adds TPWRT; a dip during the PWRT restarts it. BOR and PWRT are configured separately. The BOR re-arms the POR within the BOR range so the part stays in reset if VDD falls below where the BOR works. BOR and POR events both clear the BOR bit; set POR and BOR in software after a POR, then BOR = 0 with POR = 1 marks a brown-out. With BOREN = 01, SBOREN in RCON turns the BOR on and off (it reads 0 in other modes), though BORV still sets the level; with BOREN = 10 the BOR runs in hardware but switches off in Sleep and back on afterwards. Enabling the BOR also enables the FVR if nothing else has, and the BOR works only once the FVR is stable (FVRST in VREFCON0), which matters when enabling it in software or on wake from Sleep.

LPBOR, enabled by LPBOR (CONFIG2L<6>), watches VDD at lower current than the BOR but trips within a wider, fixed voltage range (parameter D006). It holds the part in reset at low voltage and reports through the same BOR bit (RCON<0>).

Three on-chip timers make sure the clock is stable before code runs. The PWRT is an 11-bit counter on INTRC giving about 2048 x 32 µs = 65.6 ms, enabled by clearing PWRTEN, varying from chip to chip with temperature and process. The OST adds 1024 OSC1 cycles after the PWRT, in XT, LP and HS modes only, on POR or on leaving power-managed modes that stop the oscillator. With the PLL on, a separate PLL lock time-out TPLL, typically 2 ms, follows the OST. At power-up the PWRT starts when the POR pulse clears, then the OST; in RC mode with the PWRT off there is no time-out at all. Since the time-outs run from the POR pulse, holding MCLR low long enough lets them all expire, so code starts the moment MCLR rises, which is useful for testing or for starting several parts together.

Some registers are unknown after POR and unchanged by other resets; the rest take a reset value depending on the reset type. A WDT wake-up is treated as normal operation and changes few registers. RI, TO, PD, POR and BOR in RCON are set or cleared differently by each reset, so software can tell which one happened.

Three memories: program Flash, data RAM and data EEPROM. Harvard architecture with separate buses lets program and data be accessed at the same time; the data EEPROM behaves like a peripheral reached through control registers. A 21-bit program counter spans a 2 Mbyte space; reading beyond the implemented memory returns zeros (a NOP). PIC18(L)F24K50 has 16 Kbytes (8,192 single-word instructions), PIC18(L)F25K50 and PIC18(L)F45K50 have 32 Kbytes (16,384). The Reset vector is 0000h; the interrupt vectors are 0008h (high priority) and 0018h (low priority).

The 21-bit PC lives in PCL (readable and writable), PCH (PC<15:8>) and PCU (PC<20:16>); PCH and PCU are written through PCLATH and PCLATU, whose contents move into the PC on any write to PCL, while a read of PCL copies the upper bytes into the latches. The PC addresses bytes; its LSb is fixed at 0 and it steps by two. CALL, RCALL, GOTO and branches load the PC directly without using the latches.

Up to 31 calls and interrupts can nest. The PC is pushed by CALL, RCALL or an interrupt acknowledge and popped by RETURN, RETLW or RETFIE; PCLATU/PCLATH are unaffected. The stack is a 31-word by 21-bit RAM outside program and data space with a 5-bit pointer, STKPTR, which is 00000 after every reset (a value with no RAM behind it). TOSU:TOSH:TOSL give read and write access to the top entry, so software can keep its own stack; disable global interrupts while touching it. STKPTR counts 0 to 31, increments before a push and decrements after a pop, and can be read and written, for example by an RTOS.

After 31 pushes without a pop STKFUL sets; it clears by software or POR. With STVREN set (the default, in CONFIG4L) the 31st push stores PC + 2, sets STKFUL and resets the part with the pointer at zero. With STVREN clear STKFUL sets, the pointer goes to 31 and further pushes do not overwrite the 31st entry. Popping an empty stack returns zero to the PC and sets STKUNF with the pointer left at zero (reset if STVREN = 1); returning to the Reset vector this way is not a reset and leaves the SFRs unchanged. PUSH places the current PC on the stack; POP discards the top entry, so the previous one becomes the TOS.

STATUS, WREG and BSR each have a one-level shadow, neither readable nor writable, loaded on every interrupt vector and restored by RETFIE, FAST. With both interrupt priorities in use it cannot reliably serve low-priority returns, since a high-priority interrupt overwrites it, so key registers are saved in software. Without priorities every interrupt may use it; with no interrupts, CALL label, FAST and RETURN, FAST use it to save and restore STATUS, WREG and BSR around a subroutine.

Two ways: a computed GOTO, where ADDWF PCL jumps into a run of RETLW nn instructions by an even byte offset in WREG (one data byte per instruction word, and it uses a stack level); or table reads, which store two bytes per program word, with TBLPTR holding the byte address and TABLAT the data byte moved.

The clock into the core is divided by four into the non-overlapping quadrature clocks Q1 to Q4. The PC increments on Q1 and the instruction is fetched and latched in Q4, then decoded and executed in the next Q1 to Q4, with data memory read in Q2 and written in Q4. Fetch and execute overlap, so each instruction takes effectively one cycle, except those that change the PC, which take two because the prefetched instruction is flushed.

Instructions are two or four bytes, least significant byte at an even address. CALL and GOTO hold an absolute word address written to PC<20:1>; branch offsets count single-word instructions. The four two-word instructions (CALL, MOVFF, GOTO, LFSR) carry 1111 in the top four bits of the second word with 12 bits of literal data; executed alone, as after a skip, that word is a NOP.

Data memory is static RAM with 12-bit addresses, up to 4096 bytes, in 16 banks of 256 bytes, holding SFRs and GPRs; unimplemented locations read 0. The BSR, loaded by MOVLB, supplies the upper four address bits (only BSR<3:0> exist) and the instruction the lower eight; only MOVFF carries a full 12-bit address. Unimplemented banks ignore writes and read zero, although STATUS is updated as if the operation succeeded. The bank must be selected before each access: writing to F9h with BSR = 0Fh, for example, resets the program counter.

Banks 4 to 7 are dual-port RAM. With USB disabled they are ordinary GPRs; with USB enabled they become USB buffers shared by the CPU and the serial interface engine. Spare parts of it can in principle hold variables, but buffer allocation changes at run time, and Bank 4 holds the buffer descriptor tables while USB is on, so it must not be used for anything else then.

The Access Bank gives single-cycle access without the BSR: the first 96 bytes of Bank 0 (00h-5Fh, Access RAM, GPRs) and the last 160 bytes of Bank 15 (60h-FFh, the SFRs), addressed as one 8-bit range. Instructions with the access bit a = 1 use the BSR and the opcode address; with a = 0 they use the Access Bank map and ignore the BSR. Access RAM suits fast variables and context saving. The mapping differs when the extended instruction set is on (XINST = 1).

GPRs start at 000h and grow towards the SFRs; they are not initialized by POR and are unchanged by other resets. The SFRs, static RAM like the rest, run down from FFFh and fill the top of Bank 15 from F53h to FFFh; they divide into core SFRs (ALU, resets, interrupts) and peripheral SFRs. Unused SFR locations read 0.

STATUS holds the ALU flags N, OV, Z, DC and C and can be the operand of any instruction. If it is the destination of an instruction that affects those flags, the result is not written and the flags follow the operation instead; CLRF STATUS, for instance, sets Z and leaves the rest (000u u1uu). BCF, BSF, SWAPF, MOVFF and MOVWF change STATUS without touching the flags and are the recommended way to alter it. In subtraction C and DC act as borrow and digit borrow.

Inherent (no operand: SLEEP, RESET, DAW), literal (ADDLW, MOVLW, and CALL/GOTO with a 20-bit address), direct and indirect, plus indexed literal offset when XINST = 1. Direct addressing gives an 8-bit address in the opcode, interpreted with the BSR (a = 1) or in the Access Bank (a = 0, direct forced); MOVFF has full 12-bit addresses. The d bit sends the result back to the file register (d = 1) or to W (d = 0).

Three 12-bit pointers, FSR0, FSR1 and FSR2 (FSRnH:FSRnL, upper four bits of FSRnH unused), address the whole data memory linearly without banking, through the virtual operands INDF0 to INDF2. Each FSR also has POSTDEC, POSTINC, PREINC (change the pointer after or before the access) and PLUSW (adds the signed W, -128 to +127, without changing either). Increments and decrements carry across the whole pair and never change the STATUS flags. Pointing an FSR at a virtual register fails: reading INDF1 through INDF0 gives 00h and writing it is a NOP, while writing INDF2 or POSTDEC2 writes FSR2 without any increment or decrement.

operation.topic: Extended instruction set and indexed literal offset
operation.text: XINST = 1 adds eight instructions and the indexed literal offset mode; memory size, linear addressing and the SFR map stay the same, and FSR0/FSR1 indirect addressing is unchanged. When an instruction forces the Access Bank (a = 0) with a file address of 5Fh or less, that address becomes an offset added to FSR2 (syntax ADDWF [k], d), reaching anywhere in data memory. Byte- and bit-oriented instructions (almost half the set) are affected; those using a = 1 or addresses of 60h and up are not, nor are inherent and literal instructions. In this mode the lower 96 Access RAM bytes map to a window from FSR2 to FSR2 + 5Fh, while 60h-FFh still map to the SFRs; Bank 0 below 5Fh stays reachable through the BSR.

Flash can be read, written and erased in normal operation over the VDD range. Reads are one byte at a time; writes and erases are 64-byte blocks; bulk erase cannot be started from user code. During a write or erase instruction fetch stops and code cannot run until the internal timer ends the operation. Any value can be written; an invalid instruction executes as a NOP. TBLRD copies one program byte into TABLAT; TBLWT puts TABLAT into one of the write-block holding registers, later written as a block. Data tables need not be word aligned; code must be.

EECON1 controls the access and EECON2, not a physical register (reads 0), takes the unlock sequence. EEPGD selects program memory (1) or data EEPROM (0); CFGS = 1 selects the configuration registers regardless of EEPGD. FREE makes the next WR an erase. WREN allows writes and is clear at power-up. WRERR flags a write cut short by a reset or attempted improperly. WR starts the write, can only be set by firmware and is cleared by hardware when done; EEIF in PIR2 then sets and stays set until firmware clears it.

TABLAT is the 8-bit SFR that carries data between program memory and RAM. TBLPTR (TBLPTRU:TBLPTRH:TBLPTRL) is 22 bits: 21 bits address up to 2 Mbytes and the 22nd bit (TBLPTR<21>) reaches the device ID, user ID and configuration bits; the auto-increment and decrement modes act on the lower 21 bits. TBLRD uses all 22 bits. On TBLWT the six LSbs pick the holding register; on the block write (WR = 1) the upper bits, TBLPTR<21:6>, choose the 64-byte block and the six LSbs are ignored; on erase TBLPTR<21:6> name the block.
TBLRD places the byte at TBLPTR into TABLAT and can step TBLPTR for the next read. Memory is organized in words, and the address LSb selects the high or low byte.

The smallest erase is 32 words (64 bytes); only an external programmer or ICSP can bulk erase, and single words cannot be erased. Sequence: load TBLPTR with the block address (TBLPTR<21:6>), set EEPGD, clear CFGS, set WREN and FREE, disable interrupts, write 55h then 0AAh to EECON2, set WR; the CPU stalls about 2 ms during the erase; then re-enable interrupts. The 55h/0AAh sequence guards against accidental writes.

Programming is in 64-byte blocks only, through 64 holding registers loaded by 64 TBLWT short writes, then a long write. Sequence: read the 64 bytes to RAM and update them, erase the block, load TBLPTR, write the block into the holding registers with TBLWT*+ or TBLWT+*, set EEPGD, clear CFGS, set WREN, disable interrupts, write 55h and 0AAh to EECON2, set WR (CPU stalls about 2 ms), re-enable interrupts, verify by table read; about 6 ms per block in all. TBLPTR must point inside the block's address range before WR is set. Write timing comes from an on-chip timer, and an on-chip charge pump makes the program voltage over the whole supply range. Holding registers reset to FFh after resets and writes; writing FFh leaves a byte unchanged, so single bytes can be changed without loading every register, as long as no bit goes from 0 to 1.

Verifying written data is good practice where heavy writing stresses bits near their limit. If power fails or a reset hits during a write, check and reprogram the location; an MCLR or WDT reset during a write sets WRERR. The unlock sequence protects against spurious writes. Code protection of Flash program memory is set by the configuration bits.

A separate nonvolatile array for long-term data, reached indirectly through EECON1, EECON2, EEDATA and EEADR, readable and writable in normal operation over the VDD range. It reads and writes single bytes, and a write erases the byte first. The write time comes from an on-chip timer and varies with voltage, temperature and part. EEADR's 8 bits address 256 bytes (00h-FFh). EECON1/EECON2 work as for program memory: EEPGD = 0 selects the EEPROM, CFGS = 0 selects memory rather than configuration registers; RD and WR start a read and a write, set by firmware and cleared by hardware; RD cannot be set when EEPGD = 1. WRERR may read 1 after a write cut short or done wrongly.

operation.topic: Reading and writing the data EEPROM
operation.text: Read: write the address to EEADR, clear EEPGD and CFGS, set RD; EEDATA holds the byte on the next instruction cycle until the next read or a write to it. Write: load EEADR and EEDATA, clear EEPGD and CFGS, set WREN, then write 55h and 0AAh to EECON2 and set WR for each byte; the write does not start unless this sequence is followed exactly, and interrupts are best disabled during it. WREN, cleared at power-up and not by hardware, should stay clear except while writing; WR cannot be set without WREN and both cannot be set by one instruction; EECON1, EEADR and EEDATA are locked while a write runs. At the end WR clears and EEIF sets, to be cleared by software. Verify written values where wear matters.

The EEPROM has its own code-protect bits: protection blocks external reads and writes, but the CPU can always read and write it. WREN clear at power-up, writes blocked during the Power-up Timer period, the unlock sequence and WREN together guard against accidental writes in brown-outs, glitches or runaway code. The array suits frequently changed data; if some variables change often and others seldom, the total write count of the array can be exceeded without any one byte reaching its limit, and a refresh of the whole array is then needed, so rarely changing constants, IDs and calibration are better kept in Flash. Storing only constants or rarely changing data likely needs no refresh.

The ALU includes an unsigned 8 x 8 multiplier producing a 16-bit result in PRODH:PRODL in one instruction cycle, without changing any STATUS flag. With one operand already in WREG an unsigned multiply is a single MULWF; a signed multiply tests each operand's MSb and subtracts the other operand from PRODH where needed. 16 x 16 products are built from four 8 x 8 multiplies into RES3:RES0, with extra subtractions for signed operands.

Most interrupt sources can be given a high or a low priority; INT0 has no priority bit and is always high priority. High-priority interrupts vector to 0008h and low-priority ones to 0018h, and a high-priority event can break into a low-priority service routine already running. Thirteen registers control interrupts: INTCON, INTCON2, INTCON3, PIR1-PIR3, PIE1-PIE3, IPR1-IPR3 and RCON. A source generally has a flag bit (the event happened), an enable bit (the flag may branch to the vector) and a priority bit.

With IPEN in RCON clear, the reset default, priority bits in IPRx have no effect and every interrupt goes to 0008h, as on mid-range PIC devices. PEIE/GIEL then gates only the peripheral sources (effective when GIE/GIEH is also set), and GIE/GIEH gates every source, peripherals included.

Setting IPEN turns GIE/GIEH into GIEH, the enable for all sources whose priority bit is set, and PEIE/GIEL into GIEL, the enable for sources whose priority bit is clear. Clearing GIEH disables every source, low priority included; GIEL enables the low-priority sources only while GIEH is also set. When a flag, its enable and the matching global enable are all set, execution goes straight to 0008h or 0018h according to the source's priority bit; single sources can be masked with their own enable bits.

On entry the global enable that applies is cleared, the return address is pushed on the stack and the PC is loaded with 0008h or 0018h. Low-priority interrupts wait while a high-priority one is being served. The routine finds the source by polling the flags in INTCONx and PIRx, and must clear each flag in software before enabling interrupts again or the same interrupt repeats. RETFIE returns and sets GIE/GIEH (or GIEH/GIEL with priorities). For external events such as the INT pins or PORTB interrupt-on-change the latency is three to four instruction cycles, the same for one- and two-cycle instructions. Flags are set whatever the state of their enable bits and of the global enable.

MOVFF must not be used to change any interrupt control register while an interrupt is enabled; doing so can make the device misbehave. The IOCIF interrupt also needs the per-pin enables in IOCB (and IOCC).

operation.topic: INTCON, PIR, PIE and IPR registers
operation.text: INTCON, INTCON2 and INTCON3 hold enable, priority and flag bits and are read/write. PIR1-PIR3 hold the peripheral interrupt flags, PIE1-PIE3 their enables and IPR1-IPR3 their priorities. With IPEN = 0, PEIE/GIEL must be set for any peripheral interrupt to be enabled; the IPR priority bits work only with IPEN = 1.

operation.topic: INT0, INT1 and INT2 pin interrupts
operation.text: RB0/INT0, RB1/INT1 and RB2/INT2 are edge-triggered: INTEDGx in INTCON2 set selects the rising edge, clear the falling edge. A valid edge sets INTxF; INTxE masks it, and the flag is cleared in software before the interrupt is re-enabled. Any of the three can wake the device from Idle or Sleep if its INTxE was set beforehand, and with GIE/GIEH set the device then branches to the vector. INT1IP and INT2IP in INTCON3 set the priority of INT1 and INT2; INT0 is always high priority.

TMR0IF is set on overflow of TMR0 from FFh to 00h in 8-bit mode (the default) or of TMR0H:TMR0L from FFFFh to 0000h in 16-bit mode. TMR0IE in INTCON enables it and TMR0IP in INTCON2 sets its priority.
A change on an input among PORTB<7:4> or PORTC<2:0> sets IOCIF in INTCON; IOCIE enables it, each pin must also be enabled in IOCB or IOCC, and IOCIP in INTCON2 sets the priority.

An interrupt saves the return PC on the stack, and WREG, STATUS and BSR in the fast return stack. Without a fast return the routine may need to save WREG, STATUS and BSR itself on entry (W to a temporary in the access bank with MOVWF, STATUS and BSR with MOVFF) and restore them in the order BSR, WREG, STATUS before returning; other registers may need saving too.

Up to five ports, depending on the device. Every port pin shares one or more peripheral functions, and a pin whose peripheral is enabled generally cannot serve as general I/O. Each port is run by five registers: TRIS (direction), PORT (reads the pin levels), LAT (output latch), ANSEL (analog input select) and SLRCON (slew rate). Read-modify-write on LAT works on the driven output values. Every I/O pin has protection diodes to VDD and VSS.

PORTA is 8 bits wide and bidirectional. A TRISA bit set makes the pin an input (driver off); clear makes it an output driving the latch value. Reading PORTA returns the pin levels; writing it writes the latch. RA4 shares the Timer0 clock input and the C1 comparator output (RA4/T0CKI/C1OUT). RA6 and RA7 share the main oscillator pins and are I/O or oscillator according to the oscillator chosen in the configuration word; when not port pins, RA6, RA7 and their TRIS and LAT bits read 0. The other PORTA pins carry analog inputs, VREF+ and VREF-, and the DAC output; ANSELA<5, 3:0> select RA<3:0> and RA5 as analog, the setting after a Power-on Reset. RA0-RA5 can also be comparator inputs or outputs through CM1CON0 and CM2CON0. After POR, RA5 and RA<3:0> are analog inputs and read 0; RA4 is a digital input. RA4/T0CKI/C1OUT has a Schmitt trigger input; the other PORTA pins have TTL inputs and full CMOS outputs. TRISA controls the drivers even on pins used as analog inputs, so its bits should stay set for those pins.

When several outputs are enabled on one pin, the higher-priority peripheral controls the pin; the port pin function priority table lists each pin's functions from highest to lowest. Analog inputs (A/D, comparator, SR latch inputs) are not in the lists: they work when the pin is set analog in ANSELx, and a digital output can still drive a pin in analog mode with the listed priority. This holds for PORTA to PORTE.

PORTB is 8 bits wide and bidirectional, with TRISB, PORTB and LATB working as on PORTA. RB<7:4> offer interrupt-on-change and every PORTB pin has a weak pull-up. After POR, RB<5:0> are analog inputs and read 0 and RB<7:6> are digital inputs; with configuration bit PBADEN = 0, RB<5:0> come up as digital inputs instead. PORTB pins have TTL input buffers.

Each PORTB pin has its own weak pull-up, selected by its WPUB bit. With RBPU in INTCON2 clear, the pull-ups of all pins whose WPUB bit is set are on; RBPU set turns every weak pull-up off. A pull-up is switched off on its own when the pin is an output, and all pull-ups are off after a Power-on Reset.

RB<7:4> can each be enabled for interrupt-on-change by their IOCB bit; IOCIE in INTCON enables the interrupt for all pins whose IOCB bit is set. Only inputs take part: a pin set as output is left out of the comparison. Each enabled pin is compared with the value latched at the last PORTB read, and the mismatches are ORed into IOCIF. The interrupt wakes the device from Sleep or any Idle mode. To clear it, read or write PORTB (not as the source or destination of MOVFF), which ends the mismatch, then after at least one more instruction clear IOCIF. While a mismatch remains, IOCIF keeps being set. The last-read latch is not changed by an MCLR or Brown-out Reset, so IOCIF stays set after either if a mismatch is present. A change that arrives during the read (start of Q2) may not set IOCIF, and because a port read or write touches all its bits, a change on one pin can be missed while another is being serviced. The feature suits wake-up on a key press and uses where PORTB serves only interrupt-on-change; polling PORTB while using it is discouraged.

operation.topic: PORTB alternate functions and pin relocation
operation.text: Some PORTB functions can move to other pins through configuration bits in CONFIG3H. SDO is on RB3 by default; SDOMX = 0 moves it to RC7. T3CMX = 0 moves T3CKI to RB5 and CCP2MX = 0 moves CCP2 to RB3.

PORTC is 8 bits wide and bidirectional, with TRISC, PORTC and LATC working as on PORTA, and Schmitt trigger input buffers. T3CKI is on RC0 by default (T3CMX = 0 moves it to RB5) and CCP2 on RC1 by default (CCP2MX = 0 moves it to RB3). The EUSART and MSSP override TRIS bits to make their pins inputs or outputs as they need, so TRIS should be set with care when those peripherals are on; reading TRISC always returns its own contents even while a peripheral overrides a pin. After POR these pins are analog inputs. RC<7:4> and RC<2:0> can each be enabled for interrupt-on-change in IOCC, working as on PORTB. RC0 and RC1 have no ANSEL bits.

PORTD exists only on the 40- and 44-pin devices. It is 8 bits wide and bidirectional, with TRISD, PORTD and LATD working as on PORTA; each pin can be input or output on its own and has a Schmitt trigger input buffer. All PORTD pins share analog and digital peripheral functions, and after POR they are analog inputs.

On 40/44-pin devices PORTE has four bits. RE0/AN5, RE1/AN6 and RE2/AN7 can each be input or output, have Schmitt trigger input buffers and read 0 when set as analog inputs; after POR they are analog inputs. TRISE sets their direction even when they serve as analog inputs, so they should be kept as inputs then. LATE works as on the other ports. The fourth bit, MCLR/VPP/RE3, is input only and depends on configuration bit MCLRE: with MCLRE = 0 it is a digital input with no TRIS or LAT bit, otherwise it is the device's Master Clear input; in both cases it is also the programming voltage input. After POR, RE3 is a digital input only if Master Clear is disabled. On the 28-pin PIC18(L)F2XK50, PORTE is RE3 alone, a one-bit input port available only when Master Clear is disabled.

RE3 has its own weak pull-up, selected by WPUE3 (TRISE<7>). RBPU in INTCON2 governs the pull-ups of PORTB and PORTE together: with RBPU = 0 every pin whose WPUE3 or WPUBx bit is set has its pull-up on; RBPU = 1 turns all weak pull-ups off. They are off after a Power-on Reset. When RE3 is the MCLR pin (MCLRE = 1 and LVP = 0) or Low-Voltage Programming is on (LVP = 1, any MCLRE), the pull-up is always on and WPUE3 does nothing.

Pins used as analog inputs need their digital input buffer turned off, or a badly biased digital input can draw excess current. ANSELA to ANSELE give one control per analog-capable pin: an ANSx bit set disables the pin's digital input buffer and makes reads of the pin return 0 while its analog functions work. ANSx does not affect digital outputs: with TRISx clear and ANSx set the pin still drives as an output while its input is analog, which can upset read-modify-write on that port. All ANSEL bits are 1 after POR and BOR, and so are all TRIS bits, so every pin that has an ANSEL bit starts as an analog input.
Each port's output slew rate can be the standard rate or a reduced rate of about 0.1 times standard, to lower EMI. The reduced rate is the default on all ports.

Timer0 is a timer or counter that can run in 8-bit or 16-bit mode, with readable and writable registers, an 8-bit software-set prescaler, an internal or external clock with a choice of external edge, and an interrupt on overflow. T0CON controls it, prescaler included. After a reset Timer0 is on in 8-bit mode, clocked from T0CKI at the largest prescale. T0CON fields: TMR0ON starts or stops it; T08BIT selects 8-bit (1) or 16-bit (0); T0CS selects T0CKI transitions (1) or FOSC/4 (0); T0SE selects the falling (1) or rising (0) T0CKI edge; PSA = 1 bypasses the prescaler; T0PS<2:0> set the prescale from 1:2 (000) to 1:256 (111) in powers of two.

With T0CS = 0 (timer mode) Timer0 counts every instruction clock unless a prescaler is assigned. A write to TMR0 stops counting for two instruction cycles, which the value written can allow for. With T0CS = 1 (counter mode) it counts each rising or falling edge on RA4/T0CKI as chosen by T0SE (clear for rising). An external clock must meet the T0CKI timing requirements so it can be synchronized to the internal phase clock, and there is a delay from synchronization to the count.

In 16-bit mode TMR0H is a buffer of the true high byte, which cannot be read or written directly. Reading TMR0L loads TMR0H with the high byte at that instant, so all 16 bits are read without a rollover between the two bytes. Likewise a write to TMR0L loads the high byte from TMR0H, so all 16 bits update together; writing TMR0H alone changes nothing in the timer.

The 8-bit prescaler counter cannot be read or written; PSA and T0PS<2:0> set its assignment and ratio. With PSA clear it is assigned to Timer0, at 1:2 to 1:256 in powers of two. While assigned, any instruction that writes TMR0 (CLRF, MOVWF, BSF and so on) clears the prescaler count but leaves its assignment unchanged. The assignment can be changed by software at any time while running.

Overflow of TMR0 (FFh to 00h in 8-bit mode, FFFFh to 0000h in 16-bit mode) sets TMR0IF; TMR0IE in INTCON masks it, and TMR0IF must be cleared in software before the interrupt is re-enabled. Timer0 stops in Sleep, so its interrupt cannot wake the device.

Timer1 and Timer3 are 16-bit timer/counters (TMRxH:TMRxL) with an internal or external clock, a 2-bit prescaler, a dedicated 32 kHz secondary oscillator, optional synchronized comparator outputs, several gate (count enable) sources with selectable polarity, gate toggle and single-pulse modes, gate value status and a gate event interrupt. They interrupt on overflow, can wake the device on overflow (external clock, asynchronous mode only), support 16-bit read/write, serve as the time base of capture/compare and work with the CCP/ECCP special event trigger. The TxCKI input uses a high-speed ST buffer; the register counts on the rising edge; synchronization stops in Sleep. T1CKI cannot be used while the secondary oscillator is on (SOSCGO = 1 or SOSCEN = 1), nor T3CKI unless T3CMX = 1. The synchronized comparator output should not be combined with a synchronized TxCKI.

Writes to TMRxH or TMRxL update the counter directly. With an internal clock the module is a timer counting every instruction cycle; with an external clock it can be a timer or a counter, counting each selected edge. TMRxON in TxCON and TMRxGE in TxGCON enable it.

TMRxCS<1:0> and SOSCEN in TxCON pick the clock. The secondary oscillator can clock Timer1 and Timer3 at the same time; any SOSCEN bit turns it on and selects it for that timer. With the internal clock the count advances on multiples of FOSC set by the prescaler. With FOSC itself selected the register advances four counts per instruction cycle, so a read has a 2 LSB resolution error; full resolution needs an asynchronous signal gating the clock, from the TxG pin or from comparator C1 or C2. With the external clock the count advances on the rising edge of TxCKI, synchronized to the system clock or asynchronous; a 32.768 kHz crystal on the secondary oscillator can serve as a timer clock. Counting needs one falling edge ahead of the first counted rising edge after the timer is enabled after POR, after a write to TMRxH or TMRxL, after the timer is disabled, or when it was disabled with TxCKI high and enabled with TxCKI low.
TxCKPS in TxCON divides the clock by 1, 2, 4 or 8. The prescale counter cannot be read or written and is cleared by a write to TMRxH or TMRxL.

A low-power 32.768 kHz oscillator sits between SOSCI (input) and SOSCO (amplifier output), for use with an external 32.768 kHz crystal. It is turned on by SOSCEN in TxCON, by SOSCGO in OSCCON2, or by choosing it as system clock (SCS<1:0> = 01 in OSCCON), and keeps running in Sleep whatever TxSYNC is. It needs time to start and settle, so SOSCEN should be set and a delay allowed before the timer is enabled.

With TxSYNC in TxCON set, the external clock is not synchronized and the timer counts asynchronously to the internal phase clocks; with an external clock it keeps running in Sleep and its overflow interrupt can wake the device. Switching from synchronous to asynchronous may lose a count, and the other way may add one. Reading TMRxH or TMRxL while running asynchronously gives a valid byte (hardware handles it), but the timer can overflow between two 8-bit reads. For writes, stop the timer first: writing while it increments can leave an unpredictable value in TMRxH:TMRxL.

RD16 in TxCON set makes all 16 bits move at once through a TMRxH buffer. Reading TMRxL loads the buffer with TMRxH at the same instant, and later TMRxH reads come from the buffer, so the whole value is from one moment. Without this mode each byte is read separately and a rollover between reads must be checked for. A write to TMRxL loads TMRxH from the buffer at the same time, so the high byte is written to the buffer first. Writing TMRxH does not clear the prescaler; only a TMRxL write does.

The timer can count freely or be enabled and disabled by its gate. TMRxGE in TxGCON turns on gate enable mode and TxGPOL sets its polarity. With the gate enabled the timer counts on rising edges of its clock; with it disabled the count holds. TxGSS selects the gate source and TxGPOL the polarity of each. The TxG pin feeds an external signal. With the Timer2 source, TMR2 counting up to PR2 and resetting to 00h on the next increment sends a low-to-high pulse to the gate. The C1 and C2 outputs (sync_C1OUT, sync_C2OUT) may be synchronized to the Timer1/3 clock or used unsynchronized.

operation.topic: Timer1/3 gate toggle and single-pulse modes
operation.text: Toggle mode (TxGTM set) passes the gate through a flip-flop that changes state on each incrementing edge, so a whole cycle of the gate signal is measured instead of one level; clearing TxGTM clears and holds the flip-flop, which fixes the edge measured. Turning on toggle mode while changing the gate polarity can give indeterminate operation. Single-pulse mode captures one gate pulse: set TxGSPM, then TxGGO/DONE; the timer is enabled on the next incrementing edge, and on the pulse's trailing edge TxGGO/DONE clears itself and no further gate events count until software sets it again. Clearing TxGSPM also clears TxGGO/DONE. Both modes together measure the cycle time of the gate source.

operation.topic: Timer1/3 gate value status and gate event interrupt
operation.text: TxGVAL in TxGCON gives the current gate level, valid even with TMRxGE clear. On a falling edge of TxGVAL, TMRxGIF in PIR3 is set and, with TMRxGIE in PIE3 set, an interrupt follows; the flag works even when the gate is not enabled.

TMRxH:TMRxL counts to FFFFh and rolls over to 0000h, setting the timer's flag in PIR1/PIR2. The interrupt needs TMRxON in TxCON, TMRxIE in PIE1 or PIE2, PEIE/GIEL and GIE/GIEH in INTCON set; clearing TMRxIF in the service routine clears it. TMRxH:TMRxL and TMRxIF should be cleared before interrupts are enabled.

The timer runs in Sleep only in asynchronous counter mode, clocked by an external crystal or clock. To wake the device: TMRxON, TMRxIE (PIE1/2), PEIE/GIEL and TxSYNC set, and TMRxCS and SOSCEN configured. On overflow the device wakes and runs the next instruction, or calls the service routine if GIE/GIEH is set.

operation.topic: Timer1/3 as CCP time base and special event trigger
operation.text: In capture mode TMRxH:TMRxL is copied to CCPRxH:CCPRxL on the chosen event; in compare mode an event, which may be a special event trigger, fires when CCPRxH:CCPRxL equals TMRxH:TMRxL. A special event trigger clears TMRxH:TMRxL without a Timer1/3 interrupt (the CCP can still interrupt), so CCPRxH:CCPRxL acts as the timer's period register. For this the timer should be synchronized and clocked from FOSC/4; asynchronous operation can miss the trigger. A write to TMRxH or TMRxL at the same moment as a trigger wins.
Setting TMR1MD or TMR3MD in PMD0 holds the timer in reset and cuts its clock, for the lowest power when it is unused.

Timer2 is an 8-bit timer (TMR2) with an 8-bit period register (PR2), both readable and writable, a prescaler of 1:1, 1:4 or 1:16, a postscaler of 1:1 to 1:16 and an interrupt on TMR2 matching PR2. It can also be the MSSP shift clock.

Timer2 is clocked from FOSC/4 through the prescaler, set by T2CKPS<1:0> in T2CON. TMR2 counts up from 00h and is compared with PR2 every cycle; on a match the comparator output resets TMR2 to 00h on the next cycle and drives the postscaler. TMR2 clears on any device reset; PR2 resets to FFh. Prescaler and postscaler counters clear on a write to TMR2 or T2CON and on POR, BOR, MCLR, WDT, stack overflow and underflow resets and the RESET instruction. A write to T2CON does not clear TMR2.

operation.topic: Timer2 interrupt, output, Sleep and module disable
operation.text: The match signal feeds a 4-bit postscaler (T2OUTPS<3:0>, 1:1 to 1:16) that sets TMR2IF in PIR1; TMR2IE in PIE1 enables it and TMR2IP in IPR1 sets its priority. The unscaled match output goes mainly to the CCP modules as the PWM time base, and can clock the MSSP in SPI mode with SSPM<3:0> = 0011. Timer2 does not run in Sleep; TMR2 and PR2 keep their values. TMR2MD in PMD0 holds it in reset with its clock removed.

The family has one enhanced module, ECCP1, and one standard module, CCP2. Capture times an event, compare triggers an event after a set time, and PWM makes pulse-width modulated signals of chosen frequency and duty cycle. Capture and compare work the same on both; they differ in PWM, where ECCP adds half-bridge and full-bridge outputs (four pins for full-bridge, two for half-bridge) and can also run as a standard PWM. Register and bit names carry the module number (CCP1CON and CCP2CON belong to different modules); 'x' stands for that number.

Capture uses Timer1 or Timer3, chosen per module in CCPTMRS. An event on the CCPx pin copies TMRxH:TMRxL into CCPRxH:CCPRxL. CCPxM<3:0> in CCPxCON choose the event: every falling edge, every rising edge, every 4th rising edge or every 16th rising edge. A capture sets CCPxIF in PIR1/PIR2, cleared in software; a new capture before CCPRx is read overwrites the old value.

For capture, CCPx is set as an input (TRIS bit 1); a port write to a pin set as output can trigger a capture. Configuration bit CCP2MX in CONFIG3H places CCP2 on RB3 (0) or RC1 (1, default). The timer must run in timer mode or synchronized counter mode; capture may fail in asynchronous counter mode. Changing the capture mode can raise a false interrupt, so CCPxIE should be kept clear and CCPxIF cleared after any mode change. The timer must not be clocked from FOSC in capture mode: it needs FOSC/4 or an external clock for the CCPx event to be seen.

CCPxM<3:0> give four prescaler settings. The prescaler counter clears when the module is off or not in capture mode, and on any reset. Changing from one prescale to another does not clear it and can cause a false interrupt, so the module is turned off by writing 0 to CCPxCON and then written again with the new prescale mode (for example 0x06, every 4th rising edge). The capture timer can be clocked from FOSC, FOSC/4, the secondary oscillator or the TxCKI pin. On FOSC or FOSC/4 it does not count in Sleep and resumes where it stopped on wake-up; capture works in Sleep only with SOSC or TxCKI as the clock.

Compare uses Timer1 or Timer3: CCPRxH:CCPRxL is compared continuously with TMRxH:TMRxL, and on a match the module toggles, sets or clears the CCPx output, generates a special event trigger or generates a software interrupt, as CCPxM<3:0> select; CCPxIF is set on every match, so all compare modes can interrupt. The CCPx pin must be an output (TRIS bit clear); CCP2MX chooses its pin. Clearing CCPxCON forces the compare output latch (not the port data latch) low. The timer must run in timer mode or synchronized counter mode, and must be clocked from FOSC/4 or an external clock, not FOSC. In software interrupt mode (CCPxM<3:0> = 1010) the module leaves the CCPx pin alone.

With CCPxM<3:0> = 1011, a match sets CCPxIF at once and, on CCP2, starts an A/D conversion if the A/D is on (ADON = 1) and TRIGSEL selects CCP2 (ADCON1<7> = 0). On the next rising edge of the timer clock TMRxH:TMRxL resets to 0x0000; this reset does not set TMRxIF (that is set only on overflow) and the trigger does not take over the CCPx pins. Changing CCPRxH:CCPRxL between the match and that reset lets the timer run on without resetting, moving the next event. This mode makes CCPRxH:CCPRxL a 16-bit period register for the timer.
Compare depends on FOSC, which stops in Sleep, so compare mode does not work properly in Sleep.

A PWM output switches a load fully on and off quickly; the high part of each cycle is the pulse width, set in steps, and the period is one full on-plus-off cycle. Resolution is the largest number of steps in one period, and duty cycle is the on fraction from 0% (off) to 100% (on). The standard PWM, the same on CCP and ECCP, gives up to 10 bits of resolution on the CCPx pin, set by PR2, T2CON, CCPRxL and CCPxCON. The TRIS bit must be clear for the output to reach the pin, and clearing CCPxCON gives up the pin. In PWM mode CCPRxH is read only.

1. Set the CCPx pin's TRIS bit to turn its driver off. 2. Load PR2 with the period. 3. Write CCPxCON for PWM mode. 4. Load CCPRxL and DCxB<1:0> with the duty cycle. 5. Clear TMR2IF, set the Timer2 prescale in T2CKPS and start Timer2 with TMR2ON. 6. Wait for TMR2IF (timer overflow), then clear the TRIS bit to enable the output. Step 5 is what makes the first output a complete period and duty cycle; it can be skipped when that does not matter.

PR2 sets the period. When TMR2 equals PR2, on the next increment TMR2 clears, the CCPx pin goes high (not when the duty cycle is 0%) and the duty cycle is latched from CCPRxL into CCPRxH. The Timer2 postscaler does not affect the PWM frequency. The duty cycle is a 10-bit value: eight MSbs in CCPRxL and two LSbs in DCxB<1:0> of CCPxCON, writable at any time but latched into CCPRxH only at the end of the period. CCPRxH and a 2-bit internal latch double-buffer it for glitch-free output. TMR2 is extended by two bits from the internal system clock (with prescale 1:1) or from the prescaler to make the 10-bit time base; when it matches CCPRxH plus the 2-bit latch, the CCPx pin goes low.
