Resolution is the number of duty cycle steps in a period: 10 bits gives 1024 steps, 8 bits 256. It depends on PR2 and reaches 10 bits at PR2 = 255. A pulse width longer than the period leaves the PWM pin(s) unchanged.

operation.topic: PWM in Sleep, clock changes and reset
operation.text: In Sleep TMR2 stops and the module's state is frozen; a pin being driven keeps its level, and TMR2 resumes from where it was on wake-up. The PWM frequency follows the system clock, so changing the clock changes it. Any reset makes all ports inputs and returns the CCP registers to their reset values.

ECCP1's enhanced PWM drives up to four pins, PxA to PxD, with up to 10 bits of resolution; period, duty cycle and resolution come from PR2, T2CON, CCPRxL and CCPxCON as in the standard PWM. ECCPxAS, PSTRxCON and PWMxCON add steering, dead-band delay, auto-shutdown and auto-restart. Output modes, chosen by PxM<1:0> in CCPxCON: single, half-bridge, full-bridge forward, full-bridge reverse, and single with steering. CCPxM sets output polarity. Each output's TRIS bit must be clear for it to reach its pin; clearing CCPxCON releases the pins; pins the mode does not use stay free for other functions. On enabling, the module waits for the start of a new period so the first waveform is complete. The 10-bit time base is TMR2 extended by the 2-bit internal Q clock or two prescaler bits. PxC and PxD do not exist on half-bridge ECCP modules.

With active-high outputs: in single mode PxA is modulated; in half-bridge mode PxA is modulated and PxB is its complement, each turning on only after the dead-band delay; in full-bridge forward mode PxA is active, PxD modulated and PxB, PxC inactive; in full-bridge reverse mode PxC is active, PxB modulated and PxA, PxD inactive. With active-low outputs the levels are inverted and the relationships are the same.

Two pins drive push-pull loads: the PWM signal on CCPx/PxA and its complement on PxB. It suits half-bridge circuits, or full bridges where four switches are modulated by two PWM signals. PDC<6:0> in PWMxCON give the dead-band delay in instruction cycles before an output turns on, to stop shoot-through in the power devices; if the delay exceeds the duty cycle that output stays inactive for the whole cycle. The PxA and PxB TRIS bits must be cleared.
All four pins are outputs. Forward: CCPx/PxA held active, PxD modulated, PxB and PxC inactive. Reverse: PxC held active, PxB modulated, PxA and PxD inactive. All four TRIS bits must be cleared.

PxM1 in CCPxCON sets forward or reverse, and a change takes effect at the next PWM cycle. Four timer cycles before the current period ends, the modulated outputs (PxB, PxD) go inactive and the unmodulated ones (PxA, PxC) switch over; modulation resumes with the next period. The gap in which PxA and PxC have switched while PxB and PxD are inactive lasts (Timer2 prescale)/FOSC. Full-bridge mode has no dead-band delay, normally unneeded since only one output is modulated, except when the direction changes at or near 100% duty cycle and the power switch with its driver turns off slower than it turns on: then QC and QD (or QA and QB the other way) conduct together for T = TOFF - TON, where TON is the turn-on delay of QC with its driver and TOFF the turn-off delay of QD with its driver. Remedies: lower the duty cycle for one period before reversing, or use drivers that switch off faster than on.

Auto-shutdown forces the PWM pins to a set state on an external shutdown event, to protect the application. ECCPxAS selects the sources: a low level on FLTx, comparator Cx (async_CxOUT), or ECCPxASE set by firmware. ECCPxASE reads 0 in normal operation and 1 while shut down. On an event ECCPxASE goes to 1 and stays until firmware clears it or auto-restart does, and the enabled pins go at once (asynchronously) to their shutdown state. Pins are paired PxA/PxC and PxB/PxD; PSSxAC<1:0> and PSSxBD<1:0> set each pair to drive 1, drive 0 or tri-state. The shutdown input is level-sensitive and lasts as long as the level; ECCPxASE cannot be written while the condition persists; after the condition ends and the PWM restarts (by firmware or auto-restart) the signal always resumes at the start of the next period.

PxRSEN in PWMxCON set makes the PWM restart by itself: ECCPxASE stays set while the shutdown condition is active and is cleared by hardware when it goes away, and normal operation resumes. With PxRSEN = 0, firmware must clear ECCPxASE after the event ends before the PWM resumes.

In half-bridge circuits with both switches modulated, the switches usually turn off slower than they turn on, so switching both at once can leave both briefly on and short the supply through them. Half-bridge mode has a digital dead-band delay applied on each transition from inactive to active. The low seven bits of PWMxCON set it in instruction cycles (TCY, 4 TOSC).

In single output mode (CCPxM<3:2> = 11, PxM<1:0> = 00) steering routes the PWM signal to any one or more of the four pins at once, chosen by STRxA to STRxD in PSTRxCON; at least one must be set for a single output. Unsteered pins carry their port data. Each pin's TRIS bit must be 0 for the signal to appear. While steering is on, CCPxM<1:0> set the polarity of the PxA to PxD outputs. Auto-shutdown applies to steering mode too and affects only pins with PWM enabled. STRxSYNC = 0 changes steering as soon as the PSTRxCON write instruction completes, which can leave an incomplete waveform but removes a signal at once; STRxSYNC = 1 changes it at the start of the next period, so waveforms are always complete.

The PWM output pins need suitable external pull-up and/or pull-down resistors. CCPxM<1:0> set each output pair's polarity (high or low active) (PxA/PxC and PxB/PxD); polarity must be set before the output drivers are enabled, and changing it with the drivers on can damage the application circuit. The output latches may be in the wrong state when the module starts, so the mode should be set and a full PWM cycle completed (TMR2IF set as the second period begins) before the pin drivers are enabled. Out of reset every I/O pin is high impedance, so external circuits must hold the power switches off until the device drives the pins or starts the PWM.

1. Set the TRIS bits of the PWM pins in use (P1A to P1D) so they are inputs during setup, and set their PSTR1CON bits. 2. Load PR2 with the period. 3. Turn auto-shutdown off or pick its source with CCP1AS<2:0> in ECCP1AS. 4. Prepare the shutdown sources: configure each comparator used with its inputs analog, or configure FLT0 and clear ANSB0. 5. Force a shutdown (OFF included): set the safe drive states with PSS1AC<1:0> and PSS1BD<1:0>, clear P1RSEN in PWM1CON and set CCP1AS in ECCP1AS. 6. Write CCP1CON with the output configuration and direction (P1M<1:0>) and polarities (CCP1M<3:0>). 7. Load the duty cycle: eight MSbs in CCPR1L, two LSbs in DC<1:0> of CCP1CON. 8. In half-bridge mode load the dead-band delay into P1DC<6:0> of PWM1CON. 9. Set the TMR2 prescale in T2CKPS and set TMR2ON. 10. Clear the TRIS bits of the outputs used. 11. Start the PWM: set P1RSEN if auto-restart is wanted, otherwise clear CCP1ASE in ECCP1AS.

The Master Synchronous Serial Port is a synchronous serial interface for talking to other chips such as serial EEPROMs, shift registers, display drivers and A/D converters. It runs either as SPI or as I2C. In SPI it offers master and slave operation, a choice of clock polarity, slave-select synchronisation in slave operation and daisy-chained slaves. In I2C it offers master and slave operation, byte NACKing as a slave, limited multi-master support, 7-bit and 10-bit addresses, interrupts on Start and Stop with masking, stretching of the clock, detection of bus collisions, general call address matching, address masking, address and data hold modes, and a selectable SDA hold time.

SPI is a full-duplex synchronous bus with one master and one or more slaves, using four signals: the clock SCK, data output SDO, data input SDI and slave select SS. Each slave needs its own select line from the master, and only one slave is selected at a time; unselected slaves leave their outputs high impedance and ignore the clock and data. The master and the slave each hold an 8-bit shift register. Data leaves MSb first on one clock edge and is latched on the other, so after eight clocks the two registers have swapped contents. Master SDO goes to slave SDI and slave SDO to master SDI; both ends must use the same clock polarity. A transfer may last any number of clocks; when it is done the master stops the clock and deselects the slave.

SPI uses SSPxSTAT, SSPxCON1, SSPxCON3, SSPxBUF, SSPxADD and the shift register SSPxSR, which software cannot reach directly. SSPxCON1<5:0> and SSPxSTAT<7:6> set master or slave operation (SCK is an output as master and an input as slave), clock polarity (the idle level of SCK), input sample phase (middle or end of the data output time), the clock edge data changes on, the clock rate (master only) and slave-select handling (slave only). In one master mode SSPxADD feeds the baud rate generator. Setting SSPxEN turns the port on and gives SDI, SDO, SCK and SS to it; to change the setup, clear SSPxEN, rewrite the control registers and set it again. TRIS settings: SDI input, SDO output, SCK output as master and input as slave, SS input. A function that is not needed can be taken back by setting its TRIS bit the other way.

A received byte moves from SSPxSR to SSPxBUF, setting BF in SSPxSTAT and the SSPIF flag, so the next byte can arrive before the last one is read: reception is double-buffered. Transmission is not: a write to SSPxBUF goes to SSPxSR as well. A write to SSPxBUF while a transfer is under way is ignored and sets WCOL in SSPxCON1, which software must clear before further writes succeed. When receiving, read SSPxBUF before writing the next byte; reading it clears BF. The MSSP interrupt, or polling, tells when a transfer is complete.

The master starts a transfer whenever it writes SSPxBUF, since it owns SCK. To receive only, SDO can be turned into an input; SSPxSR keeps shifting in SDI at the set rate and each byte lands in SSPxBUF with the usual flags. Clock polarity comes from CKP in SSPxCON1 and the edge from CKE in SSPxSTAT; MSb goes first. With CKE set, SDO is valid before the first SCK edge. SMP selects where the input is sampled. The bit rate is one of FOSC/4 (TCY), FOSC/16 (4 TCY), FOSC/64 (16 TCY), the Timer2 output divided by 2, or FOSC/(4 × (SSPxADD + 1)).

As a slave the port shifts on external SCK pulses and sets SSPIF when the last bit is latched. Before the module is enabled in slave mode the clock line must already sit at its idle level, which CKP sets; the SCK pin can be read to check it. The external clock's high and low times must each be at least the minimum given in the electrical specifications. A slave keeps transmitting and receiving in Sleep, clocked from SCK, and a received byte raises an interrupt that can wake the device.

Slaves can be chained: the first slave's output feeds the second slave's input and so on, and the last slave's output returns to the master. During each later group of clocks a slave sends out what it took in during the group before, so the chain behaves as one long shift register and needs a single select line. Only the latest byte on the bus matters to a slave in a chain; setting BOEN in SSPxCON3 lets SSPxBUF be written even when the previous byte was not read, so data meant for others can be skipped.

In slave mode with SS control (SSPxCON1<3:0> = 0100) the SS line frames transfers: the master holds it high until it is ready and pulls it low to start. If the slave mis-receives, it is reset when SS goes high at the end, and is ready again at the next low; without SS a missed bit leaves the slave one bit out of step for every later transfer. With SS low the port transmits, receives and drives SDO; when SS goes high SDO stops being driven at once, even mid-byte, and floats, so external pull-up or pull-down resistors may be wanted. The module resets if SS is taken to VDD in this mode. SS control must be enabled when the slave runs with CKE set, and SMP must stay clear in slave mode. A reset of the SPI, by SS high or by clearing SSPxEN, forces the bit counter to 0.

In master mode the module clock may differ from the full-power clock, and in Sleep every clock stops; take care when the MSSP clock runs far above the system clock. A master in Sleep holds the transfer where it is and carries on after wake-up. A slave's shift register runs from SCK independently of the device clock, so bytes can be shifted in during Sleep; after eight bits the MSSP flag is set and, when enabled, its interrupt wakes the device. Disable MSSP interrupts if no wake-up is wanted.

I2C is a multi-master bus of two signals, serial clock SCL and serial data SDA, both bidirectional and open-drain with pull-up resistors to the supply; a line pulled to ground is a 0 and a released line is a 1. Slaves are reached by address. A device can be master transmitter, master receiver, slave transmitter or slave receiver. A master begins in transmit, sends a Start, the 7-bit slave address MSb first and a read/write bit (1 to read, 0 to write). An addressed slave answers with an active-low acknowledge (ACK) and the two carry on in complementary directions, the receiver acknowledging every byte. Data changes only while SCL is low; SDA changing while SCL is high marks Start (high to low) and Stop (low to high). A receiving master ends with a Stop in place of the last ACK, or keeps the bus with a repeated Start. The bus defines three messages: a master writing to a slave, a master reading from a slave, and a combined message of two or more reads or writes to one or more slaves.

A device that releases a line while another holds it low sees that the line is not high. On SCL this is clock stretching: an addressed slave not ready to go on holds SCL low after a bit, and the master waits until it is released, so a slow receiver controls the flow. On SDA it is arbitration: every master watches the bus for Start and Stop and may not begin while the bus is busy; if two start together, each compares SDA with what it is driving, and the first to see a mismatch loses, stops driving SDA (and SCL, if a master) and waits for a Stop before retrying, while the winner carries on undisturbed. Slave transmitters can be arbitrated too when one address reaches several slaves. When both are still sending addresses, the lower address wins; with the same address arbitration runs on into the data.

All MSSP I2C traffic is byte oriented, MSb first, handled through six SFRs and two interrupt flags. Each transfer is 9 bits: a byte and an acknowledge. After the 8th falling edge of SCL the sender turns SDA into an input and reads the acknowledge on the next clock. The master provides SCL; SDA may change while SCL is low and is sampled on the rising edge. Enabling any I2C mode with SSPxEN makes SCL and SDA open-drain; set their TRIS bits so they are inputs. The data latch is tied to output 0 while an I2C mode is enabled.
SDAHT in SSPxCON3 selects the SDA hold time after the falling edge of SCL; setting it gives a minimum of 300 ns, which can help on buses with large capacitance.

Start: SDA falls while SCL is high; only a master generates it, and it moves the bus from idle to active. The module reports a bus collision at Start if it samples SDA low before driving it low, although the I2C specification says no collision can occur at Start. Stop: SDA rises while SCL is high; at least one SCL low time must come first, so SDA falling and rising while SCL stays high counts only as a Start. Restart is allowed wherever a Stop would be; it lets a master keep the bus, and resets slave logic as a Start does, ready for an address to the same or another slave. In 10-bit slave addressing a master must issue a Restart before it can read the slave: once both address bytes have matched, it sends a Restart and the high address byte with R/W set, and the slave holds the clock ready to send. After a full 10-bit match with R/W clear, a prior-match flag stays set until a Stop, a new high address with R/W clear, or a high address that fails to match.
SCIE and PCIE in SSPxCON3 add Start and Stop detect interrupts to slave modes that do not normally give them; in modes that already do, the bits have no effect.

The 9th SCL pulse of every byte is the acknowledge: the receiver pulls SDA low and the transmitter must release SDA to read it. The result goes to ACKSTAT in SSPxCON2. With AHEN and DHEN set, slave software chooses the reply with ACKDT in SSPxCON2; with both clear the hardware acknowledges. No ACK is sent if BF in SSPxSTAT or SSPOV in SSPxCON1 is set when a byte arrives. After the 8th falling SCL edge of an addressed transfer ACKTIM in SSPxCON3 is set; it works only with AHEN or DHEN enabled.

Slave operation has four modes chosen by SSPxM in SSPxCON1, in 7-bit and 10-bit address forms; the 10-bit forms work like the 7-bit ones with extra steps. The modes with Start and Stop interrupts also set SSPIF on Start, Restart and Stop. SSPxADD holds the slave address; the first byte after a Start or Restart is compared with it, and on a match the byte goes to SSPxBUF and an interrupt follows. A mismatch leaves the module idle with no sign to software. The SSPxMSK register shapes the match. With 7-bit addresses the byte's LSb is ignored in the compare.

The first byte is compared with 11110 A9 A8 0, where A9 and A8 are the two address MSbs, held in bits 2 and 1 of SSPxADD. Once the high byte is acknowledged, UA goes high and the module keeps SCL low until software writes the low address into SSPxADD. The low byte is then compared on all eight bits; match or no match, the module sets SSPIF and UA and keeps SCL low until SSPxADD is rewritten with the high byte, which clears UA. Every 10-bit exchange opens as a write in which both address bytes match; once fully addressed, the slave can be read by a Restart and the high address with R/W set.

A matching address with R/W clear clears R/W in SSPxSTAT, goes to SSPxBUF and is acknowledged. An overflow (BF or SSPOV set) gives a not-acknowledge; BOEN in SSPxCON3 changes this. Each data byte raises an MSSP interrupt; software clears SSPIF. With SEN in SSPxCON2 set, SCL is held low after every received byte until software sets CKP in SSPxCON1. A typical 7-bit sequence: Start sets S (and SSPIF if Start interrupts are on); the matching address is acknowledged and SSPIF set; software clears SSPIF and reads the address from SSPxBUF, clearing BF; with SEN set it sets CKP to free SCL; each data byte is acknowledged, sets SSPIF and is read from SSPxBUF; the master's Stop sets P and the bus goes idle.

operation.topic: I2C slave reception with address and data hold
operation.text: With AHEN and DHEN set the slave gets an extra interrupt and clock stretch after the 8th falling SCL edge of the address and of each data byte, so software rather than hardware decides whether to acknowledge; this adds PMBus support. Sequence: a matching address sets SSPIF and clears CKP on its 8th falling edge; software clears SSPIF, checks ACKTIM to tell whether the interrupt came before or after the ACK, reads SSPxBUF (clearing BF), writes ACKDT and sets CKP to release the clock. SSPIF is set after an ACK but not after a NACK; with SEN set the hardware stretches the clock after the ACK as well. The same holds for each data byte. Even without stretching and with BF clear, the 9th falling edge sets SSPIF;  only a NACK to the master leaves it clear. The exchange ends when the slave sends ACK = 1 or the master sends Stop; with Stop interrupts off, the slave sees the Stop only by polling P in SSPxSTAT.

A matching address with R/W set sets R/W in SSPxSTAT, goes to SSPxBUF and is acknowledged on the 9th bit; the hardware then clears CKP and holds SCL low so the master cannot clock again until data is ready. Software loads SSPxBUF (which loads SSPxSR) and sets CKP; the eight bits leave on the falling edges of SCL so SDA is steady while SCL is high. The master's acknowledge is latched on the 9th rising edge into ACKSTAT: a not-acknowledge ends the transfer and the slave goes idle until the next Start; an acknowledge means the next byte must be loaded and CKP set again. Each byte raises an MSSP interrupt, with SSPIF set on the 9th falling edge. Of all the status bits, ACKSTAT alone changes on the 9th rising edge instead of a falling edge. If the master does not acknowledge, the clock is not held but SSPIF is still set.
If a slave answering a read request detects a bus collision while SBCDE in SSPxCON3 is set, BCLIF is set; the slave drops to idle until it is next addressed, and software can use BCLIF to handle it.

operation.topic: I2C slave transmission with address hold
operation.text: With AHEN set the slave stretches the clock and interrupts after the 8th falling edge of a matching read address, so software can check ACKTIM, R/W and D/A, read the address, choose ACK or NACK with ACKDT and set CKP. After the ACK, with R/W set, the hardware clears CKP again and sets SSPIF; software then loads SSPxBUF (not before the ACK) and sets CKP. The master's acknowledge of each byte goes to ACKSTAT. The master must not-acknowledge the last byte so the slave releases SCL and the master can send Stop.

Sequence: Start sets S; the matching high address with R/W clear sets UA; the slave acknowledges and sets SSPIF; software clears SSPIF, reads SSPxBUF and writes the low address to SSPxADD, which releases SCL. The low address byte sets UA, is acknowledged and sets SSPIF; software reads it and writes the high address back into SSPxADD. Each data byte then sets SSPIF, and with SEN set CKP is cleared and the clock held until software sets CKP. SSPxADD may not be written before the ACK sequence ends. A low address mismatch still sets SSPIF and UA, letting software put the high address back; BF stays clear and CKP is unchanged. With AHEN or DHEN set, 10-bit reception behaves as the 7-bit modes do, apart from the SSPxADD updates that UA calls for.

Any time CKP in SSPxCON1 is cleared the module waits for SCL to go low and then holds it; setting CKP releases it. Stretching by a slave is invisible to the master's software. After the ACK of a read request the hardware clears CKP so SSPxBUF can be loaded; with SEN set the clock is stretched after every ACK. BF does not decide whether the clock is stretched, and the clock is now always stretched for read requests. In 10-bit mode SCL is always held while UA is set, the only stretch that leaves CKP set, and is released as soon as SSPxADD is written; the clock is stretched even when the second address byte does not match. AHEN makes the hardware clear CKP on the 8th falling edge of a matching address byte, DHEN does the same for each data byte, letting the slave choose its acknowledge.

Clearing CKP does not drive SCL low until SCL has already been sampled low, so the slave never pulls SCL down before an external master has; SCL then stays low until CKP is set and every other device has released it. This keeps a write to CKP from violating the minimum SCL high time.

The general call address, 0x00, addresses every device at once. With GCEN in SSPxCON2 set the slave acknowledges it whatever SSPxADD holds; an all-zero address with R/W clear raises an interrupt and software reads SSPxBUF. In 10-bit mode UA is not set for a general call and the second byte is taken as data, as in 7-bit mode. With AHEN set the clock is stretched after the 8th falling edge as for any address, and the slave sets ACKDT and releases the clock.

In I2C slave mode SSPxMSK masks SSPxSR during the address compare: a 0 bit makes that address bit a don't-care. It resets to all 1s, so it has no effect until written. It applies to A<7:1> with 7-bit addresses and to A<7:0> of the low byte only with 10-bit addresses, not to the high byte.

Master mode is chosen with the SSPxM bits of SSPxCON1 and SSPxEN; SCL and SDA are then inputs worked by the MSSP hardware. Start and Stop detection raise interrupts; S and P clear on reset or when the module is disabled, and the master may take the bus when P is set or the bus is idle. In firmware-controlled master mode only Start and Stop detection is active and software drives SDA and SCL directly. SSPIF is set on Start detected, Stop detected, a byte sent or received, an acknowledge sent or received, and a repeated Start generated. Events cannot be queued: writing SSPxBUF before a Start finishes is refused and sets WCOL. In master mode Start and Stop detection is masked, and the interrupt comes when SEN or PEN clears at the end of the condition. The master makes every clock and every Start and Stop; a transfer ends with a Stop or a repeated Start, which does not free the bus. In transmit the first byte is the 7-bit address with R/W = 0 and the master receives an ACK after each byte; in receive the first byte carries R/W = 1 and the master sends an ACK after each byte it takes in. The baud rate generator sets the SCL rate.

Whenever the master releases SCL during a transfer or a repeated Start or Stop, the baud rate generator stops counting until SCL is actually seen high, then reloads from SSPxADD<7:0> and counts. SCL high time is therefore at least one BRG rollover even when another device holds the clock low.

Writing SSPxBUF while a Start, Restart, Stop, receive or transmit is in progress sets WCOL and leaves the buffer unchanged. Because events cannot be queued, the low five bits of SSPxCON2 cannot be written until a Start finishes.

Setting SEN in SSPxCON2 starts a Start: with SDA and SCL high the BRG loads from SSPxADD<7:0> and counts; if both are still high when it times out (TBRG), SDA is driven low, which is the Start and sets S. The BRG reloads and, after another TBRG, SEN clears by hardware, the BRG stops and SDA stays low. If SDA and SCL are already low at the outset, or SCL goes low before SDA is driven low, a bus collision is flagged in BCLIF, the Start is abandoned and the I2C module returns to idle.

Setting RSEN in SSPxCON2 while the master state machine is idle pulls SCL low; once SCL is seen low the BRG loads and SDA is released high for one TBRG. If SDA is then high, SCL is released, and when SCL is seen high the BRG counts again; SDA and SCL must both stay high for one TBRG. SDA is then driven low for one TBRG with SCL high, SCL is pulled low, RSEN clears and SDA stays low. S is set when the Start is seen on the pins; SSPIF only after the BRG times out. RSEN written during another event has no effect. A collision is flagged if SDA is low when SCL rises, or if SCL falls before SDA is driven low.

Writing SSPxBUF sets BF and starts the BRG; each address or data bit appears on SDA after a falling SCL edge, with SCL held low for one TBRG and then high for one TBRG, SDA holding steady through the high time and a little after. After the 8th falling edge BF clears and the master releases SDA for the slave's acknowledge, which is written to ACKSTAT on the 9th rising edge (clear for ACK, set otherwise). After the 9th clock SSPIF is set and the BRG stops until the next byte is written, leaving SCL low. BF is set by the CPU's write to SSPxBUF and cleared when the eight bits are out; writing SSPxBUF while a byte is still shifting sets WCOL, which software must clear. A slave acknowledges when it recognises its address, general call included, or has taken the data correctly. Typical sequence: SEN for Start, SSPIF at its end, load the address into SSPxBUF, ACK into ACKSTAT and SSPIF after the 9th clock, load each data byte the same way, then PEN or RSEN for Stop or Restart, with an interrupt when it completes.

Reception is enabled with RCEN in SSPxCON2; the module must be idle first or RCEN is ignored. On each BRG rollover SCL toggles and data shifts into SSPxSR. After the 8th falling edge RCEN clears, the byte moves to SSPxBUF, BF and SSPIF are set and the BRG stops with SCL low. Reading SSPxBUF clears BF; the master then answers with ACKEN in SSPxCON2. SSPOV is set if a byte arrives while BF is still set; writing SSPxBUF during reception sets WCOL. Typical sequence: Start; send the address with R/W set; ACK into ACKSTAT and SSPIF after the 9th clock; set RCEN and clock in a byte; SSPIF and BF after the 8th falling edge; read SSPxBUF; set ACKDT and ACKEN to send the acknowledge, which sets SSPIF; repeat per byte; finish with a not-acknowledge or Stop.

Setting ACKEN in SSPxCON2 pulls SCL low and puts ACKDT on SDA (clear ACKDT to acknowledge, set it to decline). After one TBRG SCL is released; once seen high the BRG counts another TBRG and SCL is pulled low; ACKEN then clears, the BRG stops and the module goes idle. A write to SSPxBUF during the sequence sets WCOL.

At the end of a transfer SCL is held low after the 9th falling edge. Setting PEN in SSPxCON2 drives SDA low; once SDA is seen low the BRG counts down, SCL is released, and one TBRG later SDA is released. SDA seen high while SCL is high sets P; one TBRG later PEN clears and SSPIF is set. A write to SSPxBUF during the Stop sets WCOL.

operation.topic: I2C in Sleep and at reset
operation.text: In Sleep the I2C slave can still receive addresses or data, and an address match or a finished byte wakes the processor when the MSSP interrupt is enabled. A reset disables the MSSP and abandons the current transfer.

In multi-master use, Start and Stop detection shows when the bus is free: it may be taken when P is set or when S and P are both clear, and with the bus busy the SSP interrupt fires at the Stop. Hardware compares SDA with the level driven and reports a loss in BCLIF. Arbitration can be lost during an address, data, a Start, a repeated Start or an acknowledge. A collision is seen when the master lets SDA float high expecting a 1 and samples a 0: BCLIF is set and the port returns to idle. A transmission in progress stops, BF clears, SDA and SCL are released and SSPxBUF may be written; a Start, repeated Start, Stop or acknowledge in progress is abandoned and its SSPxCON2 control bit cleared. Once the bus is free software can begin again with a Start; a write to SSPxBUF restarts at the first data bit. The master keeps watching the pins and sets SSPIF on a Stop.

A collision during Start is reported when SDA or SCL is low at the beginning, or when SCL is seen low before SDA is driven low; the Start is then abandoned, BCLIF set and the MSSP returned to idle. With both lines released and SDA seen high the BRG loads and counts; SCL low while SDA is high is a collision, since another master is taken to be sending a 1. If SDA is seen low during the count the BRG resets and SDA is driven early; this is not a collision, because two masters cannot assert Start at the same instant and must arbitrate on the address that follows (and on into data, repeated Start or Stop if the addresses match). If SDA is high at the end of the count it is driven low, the BRG reloads, and SCL going low during this count is not a collision; at the end SCL is pulled low.

A collision during a repeated Start is reported when SDA is low as SCL rises from low to high, or when SCL falls before SDA is driven low (another master sending a 1). After SDA is released the BRG loads from SSPxADD and counts to zero; SCL is then released and, once high, SDA is sampled: low means a collision (another master sending a 0). If SDA is high the BRG reloads; SDA falling before the timeout is not a collision, but SCL falling before the timeout with SDA not yet driven is. If both are still high at the timeout SDA is driven low, the BRG counts once more, SCL is driven low and the repeated Start is done.

A collision during Stop is reported when SDA, released to float high, is sampled low after the BRG times out, or when SCL is seen low before SDA goes high; both mean another master is driving a 0. The Stop starts with SDA low; SCL is then released and, once seen high, the BRG loads from SSPxADD and counts down before SDA is sampled.

The baud rate generator makes the clock in I2C master and SPI master modes. Its reload value sits in SSPxADD; it starts counting down when SSPxBUF is written and stops at the end of the operation, leaving the clock pin in its last state. The reload is triggered twice per period of the module clock line, at points that depend on the MSSP mode. The counter runs from FOSC/2. SSPxADD values 0x00, 0x01 and 0x02 cannot be used for the I2C baud rate generator.

The EUSART (also called an SCI) is a serial I/O peripheral holding its own clock generators, shift registers and buffers, so transfers run independently of the program. It works as a full-duplex asynchronous port (terminals, personal computers) or a half-duplex synchronous port (A/D or D/A chips, serial EEPROMs, other microcontrollers that take their clock from a synchronous master). Features: full-duplex asynchronous transmit and receive, a two-character input buffer, a one-character output buffer, 8-bit or 9-bit characters, address detection in 9-bit mode, input overrun and framing error detection, half-duplex synchronous master and slave, and programmable clock and data polarity. For LIN bus systems it adds automatic baud rate detection and calibration, wake-up on Break reception and 13-bit Break character transmission.

TXSTAx (transmit status and control), RCSTAx (receive status and control) and BAUDCONx (baud rate control) run the EUSART. In every mode the TRIS bits of RX/DT and TX/CK should be set to 1; the EUSART switches the pins between input and output as needed. A pin whose receiver or transmitter section is disabled can be used as general-purpose I/O.

Asynchronous mode uses NRZ: a VOH mark for 1 and a VOL space for 0, with no return to a neutral level between equal bits; the line idles at mark. A character is one Start bit (space), eight or nine data bits and one or more Stop bits (mark); eight data bits is the usual format, and each bit lasts 1/(baud rate). LSb goes first. Transmitter and receiver are independent but share data format and baud rate, which a dedicated 8-bit or 16-bit baud rate generator derives from the system oscillator. There is no hardware parity; software can compute it and send it as the ninth bit.

The transmit shift register TSR, which software cannot reach, takes its data from the buffer TXREGx. TXEN = 1, SYNC = 0 and SPEN = 1 enable asynchronous transmission (other bits at their defaults); SPEN makes TX/CK an output, and a TX/CK pin shared with an analog function needs its ANSEL bit cleared. A character written to TXREGx moves to the TSR at once if the TSR is empty; otherwise it waits until the previous Stop bit has gone, then moves in one TCY and Start, data and Stop bits follow immediately. TXCKP in BAUDCONx inverts the transmit data in asynchronous mode (0: high-true idle and data; 1: low-true); in synchronous mode the bit has another job.

TXIF in PIR1 is set whenever the transmitter is enabled and no character is waiting in TXREGx; it is clear only while the TSR is busy and another character is queued. It does not clear at the moment TXREGx is written: it becomes valid in the second instruction cycle after the write, so polling it immediately reads wrong. TXIF is read-only and is set whenever TXREGx is empty, whatever TXIE says; it is also set when TXEN is set. For interrupt-driven sending, set TXIE only while there is more to send and clear it after writing the last character.

TRMT in TXSTAx, read-only, is set while the TSR is empty and clears when a character moves in from TXREGx, staying clear until every bit is out; it has no interrupt, so it is polled. With TX9 in TXSTAx set, nine bits go out per character; TX9D is the ninth and most significant bit and must be written before the low eight bits go into TXREGx, since all nine move to the TSR at that write. A 9-bit address mode serves several receivers.

1. Set SPBRGHx:SPBRGx, BRGH and BRG16 for the baud rate. 2. Make RX/DT and TX/CK inputs (TRIS = 1). 3. Clear SYNC and set SPEN. 4. For 9-bit characters set TX9; a set ninth bit marks the low eight bits as an address when the receiver uses address detection. 5. Set TXCKP for inverted data if wanted. 6. Set TXEN, which sets TXIF. 7. For interrupts set TXIE; with GIE/GIEH and PEIE/GIEL in INTCON set, the interrupt comes at once. 8. Load the ninth bit into TX9D if used. 9. Write the low eight bits to TXREGx to start.

Asynchronous reception is typical of RS-232 systems. Data on RX/DT enters a recovery block, a fast shifter running at 16 times the baud rate, while the receive shift register RSR runs at the bit rate. A complete character goes at once into a two-character FIFO, so two characters and the start of a third can arrive before software must act; the FIFO and RSR are reached only through RCREGx. CREN = 1, SYNC = 0 and SPEN = 1 enable it; RX/DT must be an input by its TRIS bit, and a shared analog function needs its ANSEL bit cleared.

Reception starts on the falling edge of the Start bit. The recovery circuit waits half a bit and checks the line is still 0; if not, it drops the character without an error and looks for the next falling edge. Otherwise it waits a full bit to the centre of each following bit, samples it with a majority detect and shifts the result into the RSR. One more bit time later it samples the Stop bit, which should be 1; a 0 sets the framing error for that character. The character then goes into the FIFO and RCIF in PIR1 is set; reading RCREGx takes the top character out. After an overrun no more characters are received until the overrun is cleared. RXDTP in BAUDCONx inverts receive data in asynchronous mode (0: high-true idle and data; 1: low-true).

RCIF in PIR1, read-only, is set whenever the receiver is enabled and an unread character is in the FIFO, whatever the enables; the interrupt needs RCIE in PIE1 plus PEIE/GIEL and GIE/GIEH in INTCON. Each FIFO character carries a framing error bit, shown in FERR of RCSTAx for the top unread character, so FERR must be read before RCREGx. FERR is read-only, does not stop further reception, need not be cleared and raises no interrupt; reading the next character brings up its own FERR. Clearing SPEN resets the EUSART and forces FERR clear; clearing CREN does not touch it. If every character in the FIFO has a framing error, reading RCREGx again does not clear FERR. An overrun happens when a third whole character arrives before the FIFO is read: OERR in RCSTAx is set, the two buffered characters can still be read, and nothing more is received until CREN is cleared or SPEN is cleared to reset the EUSART.

With RX9 in RCSTAx set, nine bits enter the RSR per character; RX9D holds the ninth bit of the top unread character and must be read before the low eight bits in RCREGx. Address detection, for several receivers on one line as in RS-485, is enabled with ADDEN and needs 9-bit reception: only characters whose ninth bit is set reach the FIFO and set RCIF, all others are ignored. Software checks each address against its own; on a match it clears ADDEN before the next Stop bit, and when the message ends it sets ADDEN again.

1. Set SPBRGHx:SPBRGx, BRGH and BRG16 for the baud rate. 2. Make RX/DT and TX/CK inputs (TRIS = 1). 3. Set SPEN and the RX/DT TRIS bit, with SYNC clear. 4. For interrupts set RCIE and the GIE/GIEH and PEIE/GIEL bits. 5. Set RX9 for 9-bit characters. 6. Set RXDTP for inverted polarity if wanted. 7. Set CREN. 8. RCIF is set when a character moves from the RSR to the buffer, with an interrupt if RCIE is set. 9. Read RCSTAx for the error flags and the ninth bit. 10. Read the low eight bits from RCREGx. 11. Clear an overrun by clearing CREN.

For RS-485 style use: 1. Set SPBRGHx:SPBRGx, BRGH and BRG16. 2. Make RX/DT and TX/CK inputs (TRIS = 1). 3. Set SPEN with SYNC clear. 4. For interrupts set RCIE, GIE/GIEH and PEIE/GIEL. 5. Set RX9. 6. Set ADDEN. 7. Set RXDTP if inverted polarity is wanted. 8. Set CREN. 9. RCIF is set when a character with its ninth bit set reaches the buffer. 10. Read RCSTAx for the error flags; the ninth bit is always set. 11. Read RCREGx and decide in software whether it is this device's address. 12. Clear an overrun by clearing CREN. 13. Once addressed, clear ADDEN so all data reaches the buffer and raises interrupts.

The HFINTOSC output is factory calibrated but drifts with VDD and temperature, which moves the baud rate directly. Both ways of correcting it need some reference clock. The preferred way is to trim HFINTOSC with OSCTUNE, which changes the system clock in fine steps. The other is to change the baud rate generator value, which auto-baud detection can do automatically; its steps may be too coarse to follow a slow drift of the peripheral clock.

The baud rate generator is a dedicated 8-bit or 16-bit timer for both asynchronous and synchronous operation; it is 8-bit by default and BRG16 in BAUDCONx makes it 16-bit. SPBRGHx:SPBRGx sets the period of the free-running timer. In asynchronous mode BRGH in TXSTAx and BRG16 together set the multiplier; in synchronous mode BRGH is ignored. BRGH = 1 or BRG16 = 1 can reduce the baud rate error, and the 16-bit mode reaches low baud rates from fast oscillators. Writing SPBRGHx or SPBRGx resets the timer, so the new rate applies without waiting for an overflow. Changing the system clock during reception can cause a receive error or lost data; check RCIDL shows the receiver idle before changing it.

In auto-baud detect the roles reverse: the RX signal times the baud rate generator. The generator measures a received 55h (ASCII U), the LIN sync character, which has five rising edges counting the Stop bit edge. Setting ABDEN in BAUDCONx starts it; the EUSART state machine stays idle meanwhile. From the first rising edge after the Start bit SPBRGx counts up on the BRG counter clock; the fifth rising edge comes at the end of the 8th bit, when SPBRGHx:SPBRGx holds the full bit period, ABDEN clears and RCIF is set. Read RCREGx to clear RCIF and discard its content. In modes that do not use SPBRGHx, a 00h in SPBRGHx shows SPBRGx did not overflow. During detection SPBRGHx and SPBRGx always work as one 16-bit counter, whatever BRG16 says, clocked at 1/8 of the BRG base clock, so the result is the average bit time at full speed. With WUE set together with ABDEN, detection happens on the byte after the Break. The user must make sure the incoming rate is within reach of the chosen BRG clock; some oscillator and baud rate pairs are impossible. The counter starts at 1, so subtract 1 from SPBRGHx:SPBRGx afterwards for best accuracy. Auto-baud needs the EUSART in asynchronous mode.

ABDOVF in BAUDCONx is set if the counter passes the 16-bit maximum of SPBRGHx:SPBRGx before the fifth rising edge. The count goes on until the fifth edge, which sets RCIF and clears ABDEN; reading RCREGx clears RCIF and software clears ABDOVF directly. To stop detection before RCIF is set, clear ABDEN and then ABDOVF; ABDOVF stays set if ABDEN is not cleared first.

In Sleep every EUSART clock stops, so the BRG cannot receive a character. With WUE in BAUDCONx set (in asynchronous mode only) normal reception is suspended and the EUSART watches RX/DT for a high-to-low transition, the start of a LIN sync break or wake-up character, whatever the CPU mode. The wake-up raises RCIF, synchronously with the Q clocks when running and asynchronously in Sleep; reading RCREGx clears it. WUE clears by itself on the low-to-high transition at the end of the Break, after which the EUSART is idle awaiting the next character. The wake-up character must be all zeros, 10 or more bit times long (13 for LIN, any length for standard RS-232): a non-zero character would have its first low time taken as the wake-up and the rest received as a fragment, with framing or overrun errors after. With oscillators that start slowly (LP, XT, HS/PLL) the Break and the gap after it must be long enough for the oscillator to start and the EUSART to initialise. Check RCIDL shows no reception in progress before setting WUE, which can be done just before entering Sleep. With a long oscillator warm-up WUE may clear while the oscillator start signal is still active, so the sequence must not rely on Q clocks; the EUSART stays idle while WUE is set.

A Break, as LIN requires, is a Start bit, 12 zero bits and a Stop bit. Set SENDB and TXEN in TXSTAx and write TXREGx; the written value is ignored and zeros are sent. SENDB clears by hardware after its Stop bit, so the next byte, usually the LIN sync character, can be preloaded behind the Break. TRMT shows when transmission is active or idle. A LIN master header: configure the EUSART; set TXEN and SENDB; write a dummy byte to TXREGx; write 55h to TXREGx to queue the sync character; after the Break SENDB clears and the sync byte goes out; write the next byte when TXIF shows TXREGx empty.

A Break is recognised in either of two ways. With the BRG at the expected rate, a Break has arrived when RCIF and FERR are both set and RCREGx reads 00h. Alternatively, with auto-wake-up enabled the EUSART samples the next two transitions on RX/DT, raises RCIF, then takes in the next byte with another interrupt. Auto-baud detection is usually enabled after a Break; in both methods ABDEN can be set before the EUSART is put into Sleep.

Synchronous transfers suit one master with one or more slaves: the master makes the clock for all, so slaves need no clock generation of their own. There are two lines, a bidirectional data line and a clock, so operation is half-duplex: send or receive, not both at once. There are no Start or Stop bits. The EUSART can be master or slave.

Master operation uses SYNC = 1, CSRC = 1, SPEN = 1, and SREN = 0 and CREN = 0 to transmit or SREN = 1 or CREN = 1 to receive. RX/DT or TX/CK pins shared with analog functions need their ANSEL bits cleared, and their TRIS bits should be set. The master sends the clock on TX/CK, whose driver is enabled automatically; data changes on the leading edge so it is valid at the trailing edge, one clock per data bit and no more. TXCKP in BAUDCONx sets clock polarity for Microwire compatibility: set, the clock idles high, data changes on falling edges and is sampled on rising edges; clear, the clock idles low, data changes on rising edges and is sampled on falling edges. RXDTP inverts transmit and receive data (0 high-true, 1 low-true).

Data leaves on RX/DT, and the RX/DT and TX/CK drivers turn on automatically. A character written to TXREGx waits there while the TSR still holds part of the previous one, otherwise moves to the TSR at once and goes out. Each bit changes on the leading clock edge and holds until the next leading edge. Setup: 1. Set SPBRGHx:SPBRGx, BRGH and BRG16. 2. Make RX/DT and TX/CK inputs (TRIS = 1). 3. Set SYNC, SPEN and CSRC. 4. Clear SREN and CREN. 5. Set TXEN. 6. Set TX9 for 9-bit characters. 7. For interrupts set TXIE, GIE/GIEH and PEIE/GIEL. 8. Load the ninth bit into TX9D if used. 9. Write TXREGx to start.

Data comes in on RX/DT, whose driver must be off (TRIS set). SREN gives a single character: as many clocks as data bits, then SREN clears. CREN gives continuous clocks until it is cleared; clearing it mid-character stops the clock at once and drops the partial character. With both set, SREN clears after the first character and CREN rules. Data is sampled on the trailing edge of TX/CK into the RSR; a complete character sets RCIF and moves to the two-character FIFO, the low eight bits of the top one being in RCREGx, and RCIF stays set while unread characters remain. A slave receives its clock on TX/CK with that pin's driver off; one data bit moves per clock and only as many clocks as data bits should arrive. A third whole character before RCREGx is read sets OERR; the FIFO keeps its two characters and nothing more is received until the overrun is cleared: by reading RCREGx if SREN was set with CREN clear, or by clearing CREN or SPEN if CREN was set. RX9 gives 9-bit characters, with RX9D read before RCREGx.

1. Set SPBRGHx:SPBRGx, BRGH and BRG16 for the rate. 2. Make RX/DT and TX/CK inputs (TRIS = 1). 3. Set SYNC, SPEN and CSRC, with the RX/DT and TX/CK drivers off by their TRIS bits. 4. Make sure CREN and SREN are clear. 5. For interrupts set GIE/GIEH, PEIE/GIEL and RCIE. 6. Set RX9 for 9-bit characters. 7. Set SREN for one character or CREN for continuous reception. 8. RCIF is set when a character is complete. 9. Read RCSTAx for the ninth bit and errors. 10. Read RCREGx. 11. Clear an overrun by clearing CREN or SPEN.

Slave operation uses SYNC = 1, CSRC = 0, SPEN = 1, and SREN = 0 and CREN = 0 to transmit or SREN = 1 or CREN = 1 to receive; shared analog functions need their ANSEL bits cleared, and the RX/DT and TX/CK drivers must be off (TRIS set). Transmission works as in master mode except in Sleep: with two words written to TXREGx and SLEEP executed, the first goes to the TSR and is sent, the second waits in TXREGx without setting TXIF; when the first has shifted out, the second moves to the TSR and TXIF is set, and with PEIE/GIEL and TXIE set the interrupt wakes the device to run the next instruction, or the interrupt routine if GIE/GIEH is set too. Transmission setup: 1. Set SYNC and SPEN, clear CSRC. 2. Make RX/DT and TX/CK inputs (TRIS = 1). 3. Clear CREN and SREN. 4. For interrupts set GIE/GIEH, PEIE/GIEL and TXIE. 5. Set TX9 for 9-bit characters. 6. Set TXEN. 7. Put the MSb in TX9D if used. 8. Write the low eight bits to TXREGx to start.

Reception works as in master mode with these differences: it continues in Sleep; CREN is always set, so the receiver is never idle; SREN is ignored. With CREN set before Sleep a character can be received in Sleep; it moves from the RSR to RCREGx and, with RCIE set, the interrupt wakes the device to the next instruction, or to the interrupt vector if GIE/GIEH is set. Setup: 1. Set SYNC and SPEN, clear CSRC. 2. Make RX/DT and TX/CK inputs (TRIS = 1). 3. For interrupts set GIE/GIEH, PEIE/GIEL and RCIE. 4. Set RX9 for 9-bit characters. 5. Set CREN. 6. RCIF is set when a character is complete. 7. Read the MSb from RX9D if used. 8. Read the low eight bits from RCREGx. 9. Clear an overrun by clearing CREN or SPEN.

The ADC turns an analog input into a 10-bit result by successive approximation. The analog inputs share one sample-and-hold whose output feeds the converter, and the result lands in ADRESH and ADRESL. The reference is VDD or a voltage on the external reference pins, chosen in software. A conversion can raise an interrupt, which can wake the device from Sleep. Channel select CHS<4:0>: 00000 to 11011 select AN0 upward through AN27, 11100 the temperature diode, 11101 the CTMU, 11110 the DAC and 11111 FVR BUF2. Channels AN5 to AN7 and AN20 to AN27 exist only on the PIC18(L)F45K50.

Setting up the ADC covers port configuration, channel selection, reference selection, conversion clock, interrupt control and result format. A pin used as an analog input should have its ANSx bit set, which disables the digital input buffer, and its TRISx bit set, which disables the output driver; with TRISx clear the converter reads the pin's own output level (VOH or VOL). Conversion does not depend on ANSx or TRIS. Pins with ANSx set read as 0 through the PORT register, while pins left digital (ANSx clear, TRISx set) still convert correctly; an analog level on a digital-configured pin can make its input buffer draw current beyond the specification. PBADEN in Configuration Register 3H sets whether PORTB pins come out of reset analog or digital, through the reset value of ANSELB. CHS in ADCON0 picks the channel; after a channel change a delay is needed before the next conversion. PVCFG<1:0> and NVCFG<1:0> in ADCON1 choose the positive reference (VDD, FVR BUF2 or external VREF+) and the negative reference (VSS or external VREF-) independently.

ACQT<2:0> in ADCON2 sets an acquisition time of 2 to 20 TAD applied each time GO/DONE is set: the input keeps being sampled for that time and the conversion then starts by itself, so no wait is needed between choosing a channel and setting GO/DONE. ACQT<2:0> = 000 (the reset value) is manual acquisition: setting GO/DONE stops sampling and starts conversion at once, and the user must make sure the acquisition time has passed since the channel was chosen. Either way, at the end of conversion GO/DONE clears, ADIF is set and sampling of the selected channel resumes. With a programmed acquisition time nothing marks where acquisition ends and conversion begins.

ADCS in ADCON2 selects the conversion clock from FOSC/2, FOSC/4, FOSC/8, FOSC/16, FOSC/32, FOSC/64 or FRC, a dedicated internal oscillator. One bit takes one TAD and a full 10-bit conversion 11 TAD. TAD must meet the A/D conversion requirements of the electrical specifications. Except with FRC, a change of system clock changes the ADC clock and can spoil the result.

ADIE in PIE1 enables the ADC interrupt, ADIP in IPR1 sets its priority and ADIF in PIR1 is its flag, cleared by software and set after every conversion whether or not the interrupt is enabled. The interrupt can occur running or in Sleep, where it wakes the device; the instruction after SLEEP always runs next. To continue in line after waking, disable the global interrupt; with it enabled, execution goes to the interrupt service routine.

ADFM in ADCON2 picks the layout of the 10-bit result: ADFM = 0 left justifies it, with the eight MSbs in ADRESH and the two LSbs in the top of ADRESL, the rest reading 0; ADFM = 1 right justifies it, with the two MSbs in the bottom of ADRESH and the eight LSbs in ADRESL, the unused bits reading 0.

ADON in ADCON0 turns the ADC on. Setting GO/DONE starts the conversion at once or after the programmed acquisition delay, depending on ACQT. With ACQT<2:0> = 000 the conversion begins on the instruction after the GO bit is set, which allows a SLEEP to be entered first; the holding capacitor is disconnected from the input (typically 100 ns) as conversion starts. With ACQT<2:0> = 010 a 4 TAD acquisition comes first. The conversion then takes 11 TAD for b9 to b0, followed by a 2 TAD discharge; on the cycle after the last bit ADRESH:ADRESL is loaded, GO clears, ADIF is set and the holding capacitor reconnects to the input. Do not set GO/DONE in the same instruction that turns the ADC on.

At the end of a conversion the ADC clears GO/DONE, sets ADIF and updates ADRESH:ADRESL. The capacitor array is then discharged, after every sample, so the unity-gain amplifier always charges from the same state rather than from the previous value. Clearing GO/DONE in software stops a conversion early; ADRESH:ADRESL then keep the previous result. A device reset returns every register to its reset state, turning the ADC off and ending any conversion. After a conversion ends or is stopped, 2 TAD must pass before the next acquisition, when the selected channel reconnects to the holding capacitor.

operation.topic: ADC in power-managed modes and Sleep
operation.text: For conversions in a power-managed mode, set ACQT<2:0> and ADCS<2:0> for the clock used in that mode, start the conversion after entering it, and keep the same clock until it finishes; the device may enter the matching Idle mode during conversion. Below a 1 MHz device clock use the FRC source. In Sleep the ADC runs only from FRC; it then waits one extra instruction before converting so SLEEP can execute, lowering noise. With the ADC interrupt enabled the device wakes when conversion finishes; with it disabled the ADC turns off after the conversion though ADON stays set. With any other clock, SLEEP aborts the conversion and turns the ADC off, ADON still set.

A conversion can be started by the CTMU or CCP2 special event trigger, chosen by TRIGSEL in ADCON1: 0 selects CCP2, which needs CCP2M<3:0> = 1011 in CCP2CON; 1 selects the CTMU, which needs CTTRIG in CTMUCONH set. The ADC must also be on (ADON = 1), the channel selected and the acquisition time covered, by the user's timing or by a TACQ setting; the trigger then sets GO/DONE and acquisition begins. With ADON = 0 the trigger is ignored.
An unused ADC can be switched off with ADCMD in PMD1, which holds it in reset and removes its clock to bring its power to a minimum.

1. Port: turn off the pin's output driver (TRIS) and make it analog. 2. ADC: choose the conversion clock, reference, input channel, result format and acquisition delay, then turn the ADC on. 3. Interrupt (optional): clear ADIF, enable the ADC, peripheral and global interrupts (the global interrupt can stay off when waking from Sleep to continue in line). 4. Wait the acquisition time; a software delay is needed when ACQT gives no delay. 5. Set GO/DONE. 6. Wait for completion by polling GO/DONE or by the interrupt. 7. Read the result. 8. Clear ADIF if the interrupt is used. A sample assembly routine sets ADCON2 to B'10101111' (right justified, FRC, 12 TAD acquisition), ADCON1 to 0 (VDD and VSS references) and ADCON0 to B'00000001' (AN0, ADC on), with RA0 an analog input.

For full accuracy the holding capacitor CHOLD must charge fully to the input voltage. Source impedance RS and sampling switch resistance RSS set the charging time, and RSS changes with VDD. Sources of at most 10 kΩ are recommended, a limit set by the pin leakage specification; lower impedance allows a shorter acquisition time. After a channel is selected or changed, acquisition must finish before conversion starts. The minimum acquisition time follows from allowing a 1/2 LSb error over 1024 steps, the most the ADC can take and still meet its resolution. VREF drops out of the calculation, and CHOLD is discharged after every conversion.

The input path seen from a source VA through RS: the ANx pin with about 5 pF input capacitance CPIN and pin leakage ILEAKAGE, interconnect resistance RIC of up to 1 kΩ, the sampling switch SS with resistance RSS, and the 13.5 pF hold capacitor CHOLD returned to VSS/VREF-, which a discharge switch empties. RSS falls as VDD rises. The transfer function steps from code 000h to 3FFh across the full-scale range from VSS/VREF- to VDD/VREF+, with the zero-scale and full-scale transitions each half an LSb from the ends.

A comparator compares two analog voltages and gives a digital result, working independently of the program. Its output is low when VIN+ is below VIN- and high when VIN+ is above VIN-; near the crossing the output is uncertain because of input offset and response time. Features: independent control of each comparator, selectable inputs, output usable inside and outside the chip, selectable output polarity, an interrupt when the output changes, waking from Sleep, a speed/power choice, PWM shutdown, and programmable and fixed voltage references.

CxCH<1:0> selects the inverting input from C12IN0- to C12IN3-. CxR selects the non-inverting input: the CxIN+ pin or the internal reference CXVREF, which CXRSEL sets to the DAC output or FVR BUF1. CxON enables the comparator, CxSP sets its speed and CxPOL inverts its output. The output is latched into CxOUT (in CMxCON0, mirrored as MCxOUT in CM2CON1) and drives the mismatch logic for the CxIF interrupt, the PWM logic (asynchronous output), and, optionally synchronised to Timer1's clock with CxSYNC, the CxOUT pin (through CxOE and the TRIS bit), the SR latch and the Timer1 gate multiplexer. While C1ON = 0, C1 feeds a 0 into the XOR. Q1 and Q3 are two of the four system clock phases, and Q1 stays high in Sleep. The synchronised comparator output should not gate Timer1 together with a synchronised T1CKI.

CM1CON0 controls C1 and CM2CON0 controls C2; CM2CON1 additionally handles the link to Timer1 and the simultaneous reading of both outputs. CMxCON0 holds enable, input selection, reference selection, output selection, output polarity and speed. Setting CxON enables the comparator; clearing it disables it for the lowest current. CxCH<1:0> routes one of four analog pins to the inverting input; CxIN+ and C12INx- pins used as analog inputs need their ANSEL bits set and their TRIS bits set to disable the drivers. Setting CxR routes an internal reference, rather than an analog pin, to the non-inverting input.

The output can be read from CxOUT in CMxCON0 or MCxOUT in CM2CON1. To bring it to a pin, CxOE must be set, the pin's TRIS bit cleared and CxON set. CxOE overrides the port data latch, and CxON has no effect on that override. The internal output is latched every instruction cycle; external outputs are not latched unless stated. Setting CxPOL inverts the output, the same as swapping the inputs; clearing it leaves it non-inverted.

CxSP trades speed against power while running: its default 1 is normal speed, and clearing it lowers power at the cost of longer propagation delay. The output is undefined for a while after an input change or a new reference selection; this response time differs from the reference's settling time, and both count toward the total response to an input change. Figures are in the comparator and voltage reference electrical specifications.

CxIF in PIR2 is set whenever the output changes, detected by a mismatch circuit of two latches and an exclusive-OR. The first latch takes the output when CMxCON0 is read or written, on Q3, and keeps it until the next read or write or a reset; the second takes the output on every Q1. When the output changes the latches disagree and the XOR edge sets the flag; the mismatch lasts until CMxCON0 is read or the output returns. A write to CMxCON0 also clears the mismatch, since every write starts with a read. Because the flag is edge-triggered it can be cleared without touching CMxCON0; once the latches are cleared, a return to the earlier state raises another interrupt. Software must track the output state from CMxCON0 or CM2CON1 to know what changed. CxIF must be cleared in software, and writing 1 to it causes an interrupt. In mid-range compatibility mode the interrupt needs CxIE in PIE2 and PEIE/GIEL and GIE/GIEH in INTCON; with any clear, CxIF is still set. Interrupts work whatever CxOE is. A change in CxOUT at the start of Q2 of a CMxCON0 read may fail to set CxIF. When a comparator is first enabled its bias circuitry can give a false output: allow about 1 µs to settle, then clear the mismatch and flags before enabling comparator interrupts.

The latches can be preset before enabling: with CxON clear, CxPOL sets the CxOUT level, so set CxPOL to the desired non-interrupt level, then write the wanted CxPOL with CxON set in one instruction. The read-modify-write clears the latches during the read and applies CxON and CxPOL in the final write.

operation.topic: Comparator in Sleep and at reset
operation.text: An enabled comparator keeps running in Sleep, with extra current given in the electrical specifications; clear CxON to save power if it is not needed to wake the device. An output change wakes the device when CxIE in PIE2 and PEIE/GIEL in INTCON are set; the instruction after SLEEP runs first, and with GIE/GIEH set the interrupt routine follows. A reset returns CMxCON0 and CM2CON1 to their reset states, turning both comparators and the voltage references off.

Analog pins share the digital input's reverse-biased ESD diodes to VDD and VSS, so the input must stay between VSS and VDD; beyond about 0.6 V outside that range a diode conducts and latch-up may occur. A source impedance of at most 10 kΩ is recommended, and parts on an analog pin such as a capacitor or zener should leak very little. Analog-configured pins read 0 through PORT; digital-configured pins still convert as analog inputs, and an analog level on a digital input can draw more current than specified. Input model: source VA through RS (below 10 kΩ) to the AIN pin with CPIN of 5 pF, ESD diodes with VT of about 0.6 V, leakage ILEAKAGE and interconnect resistance RIC to the comparator.

MC1OUT and MC2OUT in CM2CON1 mirror both outputs so they can be read at once without skew; reading them there does not affect the interrupt mismatch latches. Each comparator's non-inverting input can take one of two internal references, FVR or the DAC, chosen by CxRSEL in CM2CON1 onto CXVREF and then selected by CxR in CMxCON0. CxSYNC in CM2CON1 latches the output on the falling edge of the Timer1 source clock; Timer1 counts on the rising edge, which avoids a race when the comparator gates Timer1. The synchronised output should not gate an external Timer1 clock while the Timer1 synchroniser is on, and the Timer1 prescaler should be 1:1 when synchronising.

The CTMU is an analog module for precise time measurement between pulse sources and for pulse generation independent of the system clock. With the other analog modules it measures time, capacitance, relative change in capacitance, or makes output pulses with a set delay, and it suits capacitive sensors. Features: up to 28 channels for capacitance or time (up to 17 on PIC18(L)F2XK50, set by the A/D channels available), an on-chip precision current source, four edge trigger sources each with its own polarity setting, and control of the edge sequence and of the response to edges. For time delay it connects to the C12IN1- input of comparator 2. The level-sensitive edge inputs come from the CTED1 and CTED2 pins or the ECCP1 and CCP2 special event triggers. Its outputs reach the A/D converter, the A/D special event trigger, the comparator inputs and the CTPLS pulse output.

A fixed current charges a circuit. For capacitance, current and charging time are fixed and the A/D voltage measures the capacitance. For time, current and capacitance are fixed and the voltage measures the time the current flowed. For a time delay, capacitance, current and comparator voltage are all fixed and the delay is the time to charge to the comparator threshold.

The precision current source has three ranges covering two decades, picked by IRNG<1:0> (CTMUICON<1:0>), with 01 the lowest range. ITRIM<5:0> (CTMUICON<7:2>) trims it in steps of about 2%, half the codes raising and half lowering the current: 000000 is no change, 011111 the largest increase (about +62%) and 100001 the largest decrease (about -62%).

Measurements are governed by two edge channels, Edge 1 and Edge 2, each taking its input from CTED1, CTED2, Timer1 or Output Compare 1, selected by EDG1SEL and EDG2SEL (CTMUCONL<3:2> and <6:5>). The inputs respond to level, not transitions. EDG1POL and EDG2POL (CTMUCONL<4,7>) set polarity, and EDGSEQEN (CTMUCONH<2>) requires Edge 1 before Edge 2. Status bits EDG1STAT and EDG2STAT (CTMUCONL<1:0>) are set when their edge occurs, at once if a channel is reconfigured to a level it already sees. Current flows to the outside modules only while exactly one status bit is set, and stops when both are set or both clear, so current flows only between the edges; both must be cleared, together if possible, before the next measurement. Software may set the bits too: one set turns the source on, both set or cleared turn it off.

The CTMU flag (PIR3<3>) is set whenever the current source turns on and then off, with an interrupt when PIE3<3> is set. Without edge sequencing, software reads the status bits to learn which edge came last.

1. Choose the current range with IRNG (CTMUICON<1:0>). 2. Set the trim with ITRIM (CTMUICON<7:2>). 3. Choose the Edge 1 and Edge 2 sources with EDG1SEL and EDG2SEL. 4. Set the edge polarities with EDG1POL and EDG2POL; the default is negative (high-to-low). 5. Enable edge sequencing with EDGSEQEN if wanted (off by default). 6. Choose measurement or time-delay operation with TGEN; measurement is the default. 7. Discharge the circuit by setting IDISSEN (CTMUCONH<1>), wait long enough, then clear it. 8. Clear CTMUEN (CTMUCONH<7>). 9. Set CTMUEN. 10. Clear EDG2STAT and EDG1STAT. 11. Set EDGEN (CTMUCONH<3>) to enable both edge inputs. Other modules may need setting up: Timer1 and the output compare/PWM1 module can serve as edge sources; capacitance and time measurement use the A/D converter on the channel the capacitor sits on; pulse generation uses comparator 2 and its voltage reference.

Calibration is needed for precise capacitance and time measurement and for accurate delays, but usually not when only relative changes matter, as with a touch switch whose baseline capacitance rises when a finger adds body capacitance. Absolute measurement needs two calibrations: the current source to a precise current, and the measured circuit for all capacitance other than the one being measured.

Place a precise resistor RCAL on an unused analog channel. Steps: initialise the A/D; initialise the CTMU; set EDG1STAT (CTMUCONL<0>) to turn the source on; allow settling time; convert; compute I = V / RCAL. The source can then be trimmed with the CTMUICON bits by iteration to an exact current, or the untrimmed value stored for later measurements. RCAL is chosen from the nominal current: with a 3.3 V A/D reference, aim for 70% of full scale, 2.31 V, which keeps the A/D well above its noise floor; at 0.55 µA RCAL = 2.31 V / 0.55 µA = 4.2 MΩ, at 5.5 µA 420 kΩ and at 55 µA 42 kΩ. A trimmed current or the available resistor values may call for another RCAL. RCAL should be as precise as possible for the accuracy needed; 0.1% tolerance is the recommended minimum. A sample C routine sets CTMUCONH to 0x00, CTMUCONL to 0x90 and CTMUICON to 0x01 (0.55 µA, no trim), uses AN2 as the analog channel with right-justified results, 2 TAD acquisition, FOSC/32 and VDD/VSS references, then averages ten conversions taken after 125 µs of discharge and 125 µs of charge at 8 MHz.

The A/D sample capacitor and board traces and pads add stray capacitance. With the capacitance to be measured removed: initialise the A/D and CTMU; set EDG1STAT; wait a fixed time t; clear EDG1STAT; convert; compute the offset. The result is stored and used in time measurements or subtracted in capacitance measurements. CSTRAY + CAD should be roughly known; CAD is about 4 pF. The charging time t may need adjusting by iteration to get a sensible reading, starting from a theoretical COFFSET: with CSTRAY of 11 pF and V at 70% of VDD (2.31 V), t = (4 pF + 11 pF) × 2.31 V / 0.55 µA, about 63 µs. A sample C routine uses a 62.5 µs delay at 8 MHz INTFRC and ten averaged readings.

Absolute measurement follows both calibrations: initialise the A/D and the CTMU; set EDG1STAT; wait a fixed delay T; clear EDG1STAT; convert; compute CTOTAL; subtract COFFSET to get the measured capacitance. Relative measurement, as for a touch switch, needs no calibration: an untouched switch has only the board and A/D capacitance and gives a larger voltage, a touched one adds body capacitance and gives a smaller voltage. Steps: initialise the A/D and CTMU; set EDG1STAT; wait a fixed delay; clear EDG1STAT; convert; the voltage indicates relative capacitance. A sample touch routine uses a 125 µs charge at 8 MHz, an untouched reading of 1000 counts, a trip difference of 300 and a hysteresis of 65.

With C/I known from the two calibrations: initialise the A/D and the CTMU; set EDG1STAT; set EDG2STAT; convert; compute the time between the edges. The time must be short enough that COFFSET gives a valid A/D voltage. For the shortest times select an unused A/D channel whose pin has no trace, so the total stays near the A/D's own 4-5 pF; for longer times put an external capacitor on an A/D channel and select it. Connection: edge signals on CTED1 (Edge 1) and CTED2 (Edge 2) gate the current source into the A/D converter's sample capacitor CAD, with a resistor RPR from the ANx pin to ground.

With TGEN set the CTMU makes output pulses independent of the system clock, using the comparator voltage reference, the comparator 2 input pin and an external capacitor CPULSE whose value sets the pulse width on CTPLS. Steps: initialise comparator 2; initialise the comparator voltage reference; initialise the CTMU and set TGEN; set EDG1STAT; when CPULSE charges to the reference trip point a pulse appears on CTPLS. A use is a variable capacitive sensor such as a humidity sensor: the pulse width on CTPLS follows the capacitance and can be measured with an input capture pin.

Entering any Sleep mode always turns the current source off, so an operation relying on it may not finish properly and capacitance or time results may be wrong. In Idle the CTMUSIDL bit (CTMUCONH<5>) decides: clear, the module keeps running; set, the current source turns off on entering Idle, with the same effect as Sleep. When unused, the module's peripheral module disable bit removes its clocks to bring power to a minimum.

A reset clears every CTMU register, disabling the module and its current source and restoring the defaults; it must be set up again afterwards. A measurement under way is lost, and a partial charge may remain on the circuit: discharge it by setting and clearing IDISSEN (CTMUCONH<1>) with the A/D connected to the channel before measuring again. The CTMU has three control registers: CTMUCONH and CTMUCONL (edge source and polarity selection, edge sequencing, A/D trigger, capacitor discharge and enables) and CTMUICON (current range and trim).

One set-reset latch with several selectable set and reset sources and two outputs, Q (SRQ) and its complement (SRNQ). It needs no clock. Both inputs are active high and reset wins: with set and reset high together the latch goes to Q = 0. Typical uses are oscillators, one-shots, hysteretic controllers and analog timing.

operation.topic: SR latch set and reset sources
operation.text: Each input can be driven by any mix of: firmware (SRPS sets, SRPR resets; both bits clear themselves, so one write does the job), the comparator C1 output, the comparator C2 output, the SRI pin, and the divided clock DIVSRCLK. The comparator outputs can first be synchronised to the Timer1 clock. SRSCKE and SRRCKE (SRCON1) let DIVSRCLK set or reset the latch; SRCLK<2:0> (SRCON0) picks its period.
SRQEN and SRNQEN (SRCON0) put Q on the SRQ pin and the complement on the SRNQ pin; both can be driven at once. The pin's TRIS bit must be cleared for its output driver to work.
DIVSRCLK is the peripheral clock divided by 4 to 512, chosen by SRCLK<2:0>; each pulse it makes lasts two TOSC periods through the latch's pulse generator.
A reset leaves the latch uninitialised, so SRQ and SRNQ are unknown; firmware sets or clears the latch before enabling the outputs onto pins.

A reference independent of VDD at 1.024 V, 2.048 V or 4.096 V, turned on with FVREN (VREFCON0). It can feed an ADC input channel, the ADC positive reference, the comparators' positive inputs and the DAC.

A 1.024 V core reference passes through a programmable amplifier of gain 1, 2 or 4 (FVRS<1:0>, VREFCON0), whose output FVR BUF1 goes to the comparators and the DAC. The ADC takes the reference through a separate unity-gain buffer, FVR BUF2, which is switched off whenever the ADC is not set to use the FVR.
After the FVR is enabled the reference and amplifiers need time to settle; FVRST (VREFCON0) goes to 1 when they are ready. The minimum delay is an electrical specification of the FVR.

A 5-bit, 32-level resistor-ladder voltage reference, enabled with DACEN (VREFCON1). The top of the ladder (VSRC+) is VDD, VREF+ or FVR BUF1; the bottom (VSRC-) is VSS or VREF-. Its output can feed the comparators' positive inputs, an ADC channel and the DACOUT pin. DACR<4:0> (VREFCON2) picks the level.
Because the output is a tap on a ladder between the two sources, any change in either source shows up proportionally at the output. The ladder resistor value is an electrical specification.

The DAC draws least when one end of the ladder is disconnected. DACLPS (VREFCON1) picks which end stays: 1 keeps the positive source and drops the negative, 0 keeps the negative and drops the positive.

operation.topic: DAC output clamped to a source
operation.text: To put VSRC+ on the output with the least current: DACEN = 0, DACLPS = 1, DACPSS set to the wanted source, DACR<4:0> = 11111. This is also the way to bring the FVR voltage out to a pin. To put VSRC- on the output: DACEN = 0, DACLPS = 0, DACNSS set to the wanted source, DACR<4:0> = 00000; a comparator can then find a zero crossing with no extra DAC current.

DACOE = 1 (VREFCON1) drives the DAC voltage onto DACOUT (RA2). That overrides the pin's digital output buffer and its digital input, and a read of the pin returns 0. The output can supply very little current, so an external connection to DACOUT needs a buffer amplifier.

operation.topic: DAC in Sleep and at reset
operation.text: Waking from Sleep by interrupt or WDT time-out leaves VREFCON1 unchanged; turning the reference off before Sleep lowers the Sleep current. A reset disables the DAC, takes its voltage off DACOUT and clears DACR<4:0>.

A USB 2.0 serial interface engine (SIE) for full speed and low speed, with an on-chip transceiver, internal D+/D- pull-ups, 1 Kbyte of dual-access USB RAM shared between the CPU and the SIE, and buffer descriptors that place each endpoint's buffer anywhere in that RAM. F devices also have the internal 3.3 V regulator that supplies VUSB3V3; LF devices do not. The internal pull-ups are to be turned off (UPUEN = 0) when external pull-ups are fitted. The USB clock comes from the oscillator module.

Three control registers (UCON, UCFG, USTAT) set up and manage the module, and further registers handle transactions: the device address UADDR, the frame number pair UFRMH:UFRML, and the endpoint enables UEP0 to UEP15. UCON holds the module enable, the ping-pong pointer reset, suspend control and the packet transfer disable, plus the SE0 status bit (UCON<5>), set while the bus sits in single-ended zero; watching it tells a power-up state from a bus reset.

USBEN (UCON<3>) turns the module on, resets every PPBI bit in the buffer descriptor table to 0 and switches on the internal pull-ups if they are selected, so it serves as a soft attach and detach. With USBEN = 0 all other status and control bits are ignored; set everything up first. USBEN cannot be set without an active USB clock; when the PLL is used, enable it at least 2 ms before setting USBEN so it can lock. To disable the module, clear SUSPND (UCON<1>) first: clearing USBEN while suspended may stop the module powering down fully.

PPBRST (UCON<6>) points every ping-pong buffer pointer at the Even buffer; firmware clears it, and it has no effect without ping-pong buffering. PKTDIS (UCON<4>) goes to 1 when the SIE receives a SETUP token, halting packet transfer for setup processing; firmware can only clear it, which lets the SIE carry on, and pending buffer-descriptor events stay queued in the USTAT FIFO. RESUME (UCON<2>) makes a remote wake-up: set it for 10 ms, then clear it. SUSPND (UCON<1>) puts the module into low-power suspend and stops the SIE clock; set it after an IDLEIF interrupt (setting it earlier gives unpredictable bus behaviour) and clear it after ACTVIF. While suspended the device stays attached with the transceiver outputs idle, and the VUSB3V3 voltage may change with this bit.
A typical bus-powered device may draw only 2.5 mA in suspend, counting the PIC and everything around it.

UCFG sets the system-level behaviour: bus speed (full or low), the on-chip pull-ups, ping-pong buffer use and, with UTEYE (UCFG<7>), eye-pattern generation. Speed, transceiver and pull-up are to be set while setting up the module and not changed while it is enabled.

The built-in transceiver is USB 2.0 full-speed and low-speed capable and is wired to the SIE inside; it turns on with USBEN = 1. FSEN (UCFG<2>) = 1 selects full speed. The transceiver runs from the VUSB3V3 pin, which needs 3.0 V to 3.6 V to meet USB signalling levels; 3.3 V gives the best signals, with a good ceramic bypass capacitor placed as close as possible to VUSB3V3 and the VSS pin on the same package edge. D+ and D- run straight to the connector or cable with no resistors, capacitors or magnetics: the drivers have controlled slew rate and an output impedance matched to the cable.
