Keep the traces under 30 cm and, ideally, at the cable's characteristic impedance.

Built-in pull-ups meet the low-speed and full-speed requirements; UPUEN (UCFG<4>) turns them on, and only with the on-chip transceiver enabled. A USB device may never drive current onto VBUS, nor onto D+ or D- while VBUS is below 1.17 V; a design that is not purely bus powered watches VBUS (through a resistor divider into an analog pin) and enables neither the module nor the pull-up until VBUS exceeds 1.17 V.
An external pull-up may be used instead, taken from the VUSB3V3 pin to D+ or D-. USB requires it to be 1.5 kΩ ±5%.

operation.topic: USB ping-pong configuration and eye pattern test
operation.text: PPB<1:0> (UCFG) selects the ping-pong buffer mode. Setting UCFG<7> (UTEYE) makes the module, once enabled with its SIE clock, pull-up and transceiver set up, switch to transmit and send J-K-J-K repeatedly (K-J-K-J at full speed) for as long as the bit is set. It is a board check of signal integrity for certification work, not a full certification test, and it does not exercise the receive-to-transmit turnaround; never set it while connected to a working USB system.

USTAT reports the last transfer: endpoint number ENDP<3:0> (0 to 15), direction DIR (1 for IN, 0 for OUT or SETUP) and the ping-pong pointer PPBI (1 Odd bank, 0 Even bank; valid only for endpoints with both banks). It is a window on a four-entry status FIFO kept by the SIE, so the CPU can handle one transfer while the SIE completes others. Its data is valid two SIE clocks after TRNIF is set; at low speed with a 48 MHz system clock a delay may be needed before reading it. Clearing TRNIF advances the FIFO, and if another entry is waiting TRNIF is set again within 6 TCY; otherwise TRNIF stays clear and USTAT no longer holds valid data. A request that arrives while the FIFO is full is answered with NAK.

Each of the 16 bidirectional endpoints has a register UEPn. EPHSHK (bit 4) enables handshaking, normally on except for isochronous endpoints. EPCONDIS (bit 3), with both directions enabled, decides whether SETUP (control) transfers are allowed: 0 allows them, and it stays 0 for Endpoint 0, the default control endpoint. EPOUTEN (bit 2) and EPINEN (bit 1) enable OUT and IN transactions. EPSTALL (bit 0) is set by the SIE when the endpoint issues a STALL and stays set until firmware clears it or the SIE is reset; it means nothing while the endpoint is disabled.

UADDR holds the address the module answers to; a USB reset (URSTIF) or a device reset loads 00h, and firmware writes the assigned address during enumeration. UFRML and the three low bits of UFRMH hold the 11-bit frame number, updated at every SOF token, read-only to the CPU and used mostly for isochronous transfers. They are valid only while the 48 MHz SIE clock runs (not while SUSPND = 1).

Data passes between the CPU and the SIE through 1024 bytes of dual-access RAM in data memory banks 4 to 7 (400h to 7FFh). Bank 4 (400h to 4FFh) holds the buffer descriptors; depending on the buffering mode all of it except eight bytes can also serve as buffer space. The CPU sees the whole area as ordinary RAM, but should leave alone any part the SIE is using; buffer ownership decides which side may touch a buffer.

The BDT in bank 4 is made of buffer descriptors (BDs), up to 64 (BD0 to BD63), each four bytes in the order BDnSTAT (status), BDnCNT (byte count), BDnADRL and BDnADRH (buffer start address). The table is at least 8 bytes long, because every device needs Endpoint 0 in both directions, and at most 256 bytes. BDs are not hardware registers: a BD belongs to an endpoint only once UEPn enables that endpoint, until then its bytes are plain RAM, and their content is indeterminate after any reset. Set each endpoint's BD up before enabling the endpoint. Example: a 64-byte buffer at 500h for BD0 has BD0CNT = 40h, BD0ADRL = 00h, BD0ADRH = 05h, the buffer running from 500h to 53Fh.

BDnSTAT has two layouts, one for when the CPU owns the BD and one for when the SIE owns it; UOWN (BDnSTAT<7>) is the bit they share and acts as the semaphore. UOWN = 0: the CPU owns the BD and its buffer and may set up the status, count and address. UOWN = 1: the SIE owns them, the CPU must not change them, and the SIE overwrites the BD with the token PID and the transferred count. Either side may still read BDnSTAT. Set UOWN in a separate instruction after every other BD byte is written, so BDnSTAT is the last byte updated when arming an endpoint; the SIE clears UOWN when the transaction completes. Nothing in hardware blocks CPU access to an SIE-owned buffer, and reading one may return stale data.

With UOWN = 0 the other bits are controls. DTSEN (bit 3) turns on data toggle synchronisation: the SIE checks each packet's DATA0/DATA1 against DTS (bit 6); a packet out of sync is acknowledged to the host but neither written to USB RAM nor flagged with a transfer-complete interrupt. BSTALL (bit 2) makes the SIE answer with STALL any token that would use this BD, which serves one-off stalls on Endpoint 0 and SET_FEATURE/CLEAR_FEATURE stalls on other endpoints; issuing the STALL sets EPSTALL in UEPn and raises the STALL interrupt, and UOWN stays set and the BD unchanged until a SETUP token arrives, which clears the stall and hands the BD back to the CPU. BC9:BC8 (bits 1:0) are the top two bits of the byte count; DTS is ignored unless DTSEN = 1.

Once UOWN is set the SIE rewrites BDnSTAT: bits 5 to 2 receive the PID of the last token (IN, OUT or SETUP), and bits 1:0 carry the overflow of the byte count from BDnCNT. Bit 6 is not written by the SIE. Anything the CPU had written there is replaced.

The count is 10 bits, BDnCNT plus BDnSTAT<1:0>, so 0 to 1023 bytes. For IN it is the number of bytes to send, and the SIE writes back the number sent. For OUT it is the most the buffer may take, and the SIE writes back the number received; a packet longer than the count is refused with NAK and the count is left as it was.

Nothing in hardware checks the BD address pair. An address outside USB RAM or inside another endpoint's buffer, or a receive buffer that overlaps a BD in use, corrupts or loses data; software can check the addresses.

An endpoint with ping-pong buffering has two BDs, Even and Odd, so the CPU works on one while the SIE uses the other. PPB<1:0> (UCFG) picks one of four modes: none, OUT Endpoint 0 only, all endpoints, or all endpoints but Endpoint 0. The module keeps a pointer per endpoint, set to Even when the module is enabled and toggled after each completed transaction (UOWN cleared by the SIE). USTAT's PPBI shows which bank the last transaction used, and PPBRST sends every pointer back to Even. Each BD is tied to one endpoint, so endpoints enabled out of sequence leave gaps in the BDT; those gaps should not be used as buffer space unless BD addresses are checked.

The module has its own two-level interrupt logic that ends in one flag, USBIF (PIR3<2>). The top level, status interrupts, has flags in UIR and enables in UIE: SOFIF (start-of-frame token), STALLIF (STALL handshake sent), IDLEIF (bus idle 3 ms or more), TRNIF (transaction complete; read USTAT), ACTVIF (activity on D+/D-), UERRIF (unmasked error) and URSTIF (valid USB reset; UADDR loaded with 00h). The second level, error conditions, has flags in UEIR and enables in UEIE: BTSEF (bit stuff error), BTOEF (bus turnaround time-out, more than 16 bit times of idle since the last EOP), DFN8EF (data field not a whole number of bytes), CRC16EF (CRC16 failed), CRC5EF (token rejected for a CRC5 error) and PIDEF (PID check failed); any enabled error sets UERRIF. In a frame, a bus reset raises URSTIF, each SOF raises SOFIF, and each completed SETUP, IN or OUT transaction raises TRNIF.

The UIR flags are ORed into USBIF. A flag set by the SIE is cleared by writing 0, and firmware may set flags itself to help debugging. UERRIF is read-only: it reflects only errors enabled in UEIE. Clearing TRNIF advances the USTAT FIFO (IN, OUT and SETUP tokens only). After an idle is detected the module may be put into suspend. In suspend (UCON<1> = 1) the SIE has no clock and can flag nothing but ACTVIF, which firmware uses to know when to leave suspend; ACTVIF is normally unmasked only after an idle interrupt.

ACTVIF cannot be cleared while the module is suspended or right after it wakes: the hardware takes a few clock cycles to synchronise first, and an earlier clear may not take. When the module runs from the 48 MHz PLL it may also wait for the PLL to lock after SUSPND is cleared. Firmware therefore clears SUSPND, then keeps clearing ACTVIF while it reads 1. One ACTVIF comes per resume from bus idle; after it is cleared it does not return, even with continuous traffic, until the bus has been idle long enough for another IDLEIF.
An enable bit only decides whether its flag reaches the CPU's interrupt logic; the flags are set by their conditions regardless, so they can be polled with interrupts off.

Each error flag is set the moment its condition is seen, so the interrupt generally does not line up with the end of a token. Flags set by the SIE are cleared by writing 0. All error flags are ORed into UERRIF.

The whole application runs from VBUS, the simplest arrangement. For the USB 2.0 inrush limit the total capacitance across VBUS and ground must not exceed 10 µF, or inrush limiting is needed. Every USB device must support suspend, drawing at most 2.5 mA from VBUS; the host requests it by sending no traffic to the device for more than 3 ms, which sets IDLEIF. The D+ or D- pull-up stays on in suspend and uses part of the 2.5 mA.

The application has its own supply and takes almost nothing from USB. For compliance neither the module nor the D+/D- pull-up is turned on until the host drives VBUS high, and no current may ever flow out onto the 5 V VBUS pin.

operation.topic: USB dual power with self-power dominance
operation.text: The application runs from its own supply and falls back to USB power when that is absent, switching automatically. Such designs meet both the bus-powered inrush and suspend limits and the self-powered rules: no USB enable before VBUS is high and no current onto VBUS. A device drawing from USB is limited to 100 mA as a low-power device or 500 mA as a high-power device.

Transceiver current depends on the cable's characteristic impedance and length, the VUSB3V3 voltage and the data. Longer cables have more capacitance and take more energy per transition. IN traffic, which the PIC drives, costs far more than OUT traffic, which the host drives. Data is NRZI coded: each 0 bit flips the line between J and K, and a 1 bit leaves it (bit stuffing aside), so IN data full of zeros draws the most. The SIE does bit stuffing and unstuffing, NRZI coding and decoding, and CRC generation and checking in hardware.
Full speed needs a 48 MHz USB clock; the CPU and other peripherals need not run at 48 MHz.

D+ and D- have interrupt-on-change, which can see the level change when the device is plugged into a host or hub (the host has 15 kΩ pull-downs on both lines). External resistors on each pin are needed to hold the lines high while detached. It works only with USBEN = 0; setting USBEN turns it off for both pins.

A device has configurations, each with interfaces, each with endpoints, up to 16 bidirectional; Endpoint 0 is always the control endpoint and must be available for configuration once the device is on the bus. Bus traffic is grouped into 1 ms frames. The four transfer types are isochronous (up to 1023 bytes, timely but without guaranteed integrity), bulk (guaranteed integrity, no timing guarantee), interrupt (timely and with integrity, for small blocks) and control (device setup). Full-speed devices may use all four; low-speed devices only interrupt and control.

operation.topic: USB bus power limits and suspend
operation.text: A device is guaranteed one unit load, 100 mA at about 5 V, and may ask for up to 500 mA, which the host need not grant, so a device needing more than one unit load must also have a configuration within one. In suspend the current limit is 500 µA averaged over 1 s. A device enters suspend after 3 ms without SOF tokens, must cut its current within 10 ms of suspending, and must signal wake-up within 10 ms of drawing more than the suspend limit.

On attach the host typically resets the device (address 0), asks for part of the device descriptor, resets it again, assigns an address, reads the full device descriptor, reads the configuration descriptors and any others, and sets a configuration; the exact order depends on the host. Of the eight standard descriptor types five matter most: device (one per device: maker, product, serial number, class, number of configurations), configuration (power needs and number of interfaces), interface (number of endpoints and class), endpoint (transfer type and direction) and string (optional readable text in Unicode).

A device shows its presence and speed with a 1.5 kΩ resistor to 3.3 V connected at attach: on D- for low speed, on D+ for full speed. Hosts carry class drivers (audio, mass storage, communications, HID) that many devices can reuse; a custom device may need its own driver.

A programmable detector with a trip voltage and a direction: when the supply passes the trip point in that direction, HLVDIF is set and, if enabled, an interrupt is taken. HLVDCON controls it entirely, so it can be switched off to save current. HLVDCON fields: VDIRMAG (bit 7; 1 trips at or above the trip point, 0 at or below), BGVST (bit 6, read-only; 1 when the band gap references are stable), IRVST (bit 5, read-only; 1 when the detector will flag at the set level; while it is 0 the HLVD interrupt is to stay disabled), HLVDEN (bit 4, enable) and HLVDL<3:0> (trip level: 0000 lowest to 1110 highest, 1111 external input on HLVDIN). Reset value of HLVDCON is 0000 0101. The trip voltages are electrical specifications.

A comparator compares a tap on a resistor divider from the supply with an internal reference of 1.024 V typical; when the supply reaches the trip point the tap equals the reference and HLVDIF is set. There are 16 trip settings. With HLVDL<3:0> = 1111 the comparator takes the HLVDIN pin instead, so the trip point can be any voltage in the operating range. After each enable the circuit needs time to settle, and it can interrupt only once IRVST (HLVDCON<5>) is 1. VDIRMAG = 0 watches for VDD falling below the set point; VDIRMAG = 1 watches for VDD rising above it.

Write the trip point to HLVDL<3:0>; set VDIRMAG for high (1) or low (0) detection; set HLVDEN; clear HLVDIF (PIR2<2>), which an earlier event may have left set; for interrupts set HLVDIE (PIE2<2>) and GIE/GIEH (INTCON<7>). No interrupt comes before IRVST is set. To change VDIRMAG or HLVDL<3:0>, turn the module off (HLVDEN = 0) first and back on afterwards, which avoids false events.

While enabled the comparator and divider draw a static current, given in the electrical specifications; the module can be enabled only for brief checks to save current. Its reference can be shared with other circuits such as the programmable brown-out reset. When the reference has been off it needs a start-up time TIRVST, independent of the clock, before levels are detected reliably; HLVDIF is held off until then, so a short excursion past the trip point during TIRVST can be missed. If the condition still holds when firmware clears HLVDIF, the flag is set again.

Enabled from time to time, the HLVD can detect USB attach and detach in a device running from a supply lower than USB's 5 V (a rise from 3.3 V to 5 V means attach), saving parts and a pin. On a battery, a trip point VA above the minimum operating voltage VB gives an interrupt at time TA, leaving until TB for housekeeping and a controlled shutdown.

operation.topic: HLVD in Sleep and at reset
operation.text: Once enabled the HLVD keeps working in Sleep; crossing the trip point sets HLVDIF and wakes the device, which continues at the interrupt vector if interrupts are globally enabled. A reset returns all registers to their reset state, which turns the HLVD off.

Features for reliability and fewer external parts: oscillator selection; power-on reset, power-up timer, oscillator start-up timer and brown-out reset; interrupts; the watchdog timer, either always on by configuration or under software control; code protection; ID locations; and in-circuit serial programming. The internal RC oscillator also makes possible the fail-safe clock monitor, which watches the peripheral clock and switches over if it stops, and two-speed start-up, which runs code at once while the primary clock finishes starting. All of these are set by configuration bits.

Configuration bits read 0 when programmed and 1 when left unprogrammed. They start at 300000h in the configuration space (300000h to 3FFFFFh), outside user program memory and reachable only by table reads and writes. A configuration byte is written like Flash: a TBLWT with TBLPTR on the register loads address and data, then setting WR (EECON1) starts a self-timed long write, one byte at a time; a TBLWT can write either 1 or 0 into a cell.

The WDT runs from INTRC, which starts whenever the WDT is enabled. Its base period is 4 ms nominal, as stable as INTRC, and a 16-bit postscaler (WDTPS<3:0>, CONFIG2H) multiplies it to give 4 ms up to 131.072 s (2.18 minutes). The count and postscaler are cleared by SLEEP, CLRWDT, any change of the IRCF bits (OSCCON) and a clock failure. A time-out resets the device, or wakes it from a power-managed mode. WDTEN<1:0> makes it permanently on or leaves it to software through SWDTEN.

User program memory is split into a boot block of 2 Kbytes (000h to 7FFh) and blocks on binary boundaries: three blocks in all on the 16 Kbyte PIC18(L)F24K50 and five on the 32 Kbyte PIC18(L)FX5K50. Each block has three protection bits: code-protect CPn, write-protect WRTn and external block table read EBTRn.

Table reads and writes reach program memory anywhere, and table reads also reach the device ID and the configuration registers. In normal execution the CPn bits do nothing; they block external reads and writes. WRTn = 0 blocks table writes into block n from anywhere. EBTRn = 0 blocks table reads of block n made by code running in another block, which then read 0 (TABLAT returns 0); code inside block n can still read it. Protection bits can only be changed from 1 to 0; only a full chip erase or block erase, started over ICSP or by an external programmer, returns them to 1.

CPD blocks external reads and writes of the whole data EEPROM, and WRTD blocks both internal and external writes; the CPU can always read the EEPROM in normal operation. WRTC write-protects the configuration registers; in normal execution it can only be read, and it is written over ICSP or by a programmer.

Eight bytes at 200000h to 200007h hold user identification such as a checksum. They can be read and written in normal execution with TBLRD and TBLWT or during program/verify, and they stay readable when the device is code-protected.

The device can be programmed in the finished circuit over clock and data lines plus power, ground and the programming voltage, so boards can be built blank and programmed before shipping. Programming DEBUG to 0 enables the in-circuit debugger, which then takes RB6 and RB7. Debugging needs ICSP connections to MCLR/VPP/RE3, VDD, VSS, RB7 and RB6.

On the 44-pin TQFP three otherwise unconnected pins can form a separate port for in-circuit debug and programming, with its own reset, data and clock pins (ICRST/ICVPP, ICDT/ICPGD, ICCK/ICPGC) that share nothing with I/O, leaving RB6, RB7 and MCLR free; they work like the legacy pins and have the same electrical specifications. ICPRT turns the port on; it is set by default on the TQFP and can be changed only through the MCLR/RB6/RB7 interface. With ICPRT = 1: ICRST acts as a second MCLR and needs a pull-up so the part can leave reset; the legacy pins can still program the part but debugging uses the dedicated pins; and MCLRE still works, so with MCLRE = 0 MCLR is the RE3 input and ICRST gives the reset.

Setting the LVP configuration bit turns on single-supply ICSP, which programs the part without a high voltage on MCLR/VPP/RE3. High-voltage programming, with VIHH on MCLR, works whatever LVP says. Single-supply ICSP is on in blank devices as shipped and after erase. While low-voltage ICSP is active, MCLR works whatever MCLRE says, and RE3 cannot be used as an input. LVP itself can be changed only in high-voltage programming; once it is cleared, only high-voltage programming remains. Unprotected memory can be erased by block erase or row by row and written at any specified VDD; protected memory needs a block erase.

The core runs the 75 standard PIC18 instructions plus an optional extension of eight more aimed at re-entrant code and software stacks. Instructions fall into four groups: byte-oriented, bit-oriented, literal and control. Nearly all are one 16-bit program word holding an opcode and its operands; four (MOVFF, CALL, GOTO, LFSR) take two words.

Byte-oriented instructions name a file register f, a destination d (0 puts the result in WREG, 1 back in f) and an access bit a. Bit-oriented instructions name f, a bit number b and a. Literal instructions take a constant k, and for LFSR an FSR number f. Control instructions take a program address n, the fast-return bit s for CALL and RETURN, or the table pointer mode m for table reads and writes; some take no operand.
The second word of a two-word instruction has its top four bits set to 1. Executed on its own, such a word behaves as a NOP, so every program location holds a valid instruction.

An instruction cycle is four oscillator periods. A single-word instruction takes one cycle, or two when its condition is met or it alters the program counter; the extra cycle runs as a NOP. Two-word instructions take two cycles. At a 4 MHz oscillator a normal instruction takes 1 µs, a taken branch 2 µs, and a taken two-word branch 3 µs.
Any instruction may be preceded by an optional label used for symbolic addressing: {label} instruction argument(s).

In byte- and bit-oriented instructions a = 0 selects the Access Bank and a = 1 lets BSR choose the GPR bank. With the extended instruction set enabled, a = 0 and f at or below 95 (5Fh), the instruction uses Indexed Literal Offset Addressing instead.
CALL with s = 1 also copies W, Status and BSR into their shadow registers WS, STATUSS and BSRS; RETURN or RETFIE with s = 1 restores them, and with s = 0 leaves those registers alone.
GOTO reaches anywhere in the 2-Mbyte program memory range by loading its 20-bit literal into PC<20:1>, and always takes two cycles.

MOVFF copies any of the 4096 data memory locations (000h to FFFh) to any other; either side may be W. It suits moving data into a peripheral register such as a transmit buffer or an I/O port. PCL, TOSU, TOSH and TOSL cannot be its destination. MOVLB loads an 8-bit literal into BSR, but BSR<7:4> always reads 0 whatever k7:k4 hold.
RETFIE pops the stack into the PC and re-enables interrupts by setting the high or low priority global interrupt enable bit.
SLEEP clears PD, sets TO, clears the Watchdog Timer and its postscaler, and stops the oscillator. If the Watchdog Timer wakes the device, TO is cleared.

TBLRD copies the program memory byte addressed by the 21-bit TBLPTR into TABLAT. TBLPTR spans a 2-Mbyte range and its LSb picks the byte of the program word: 0 the least significant, 1 the most significant. TBLWT copies TABLAT into one of the holding registers used to program the Flash. Both instructions can leave TBLPTR unchanged, or increment or decrement it before or after the transfer; the low two encoding bits nn select the mode (0 *, 1 *+, 2 *-, 3 +*).

Eight extra instructions (ADDFSR, ADDULNK, CALLW, MOVSF, MOVSS, PUSHL, SUBFSR, SUBULNK) and Indexed Literal Offset Addressing for many standard instructions. All are literal operations that change an FSR or use one for indexed addressing. They target re-entrant code written in high-level languages, chiefly C: allocating and freeing software stack space on subroutine entry and exit, calling through function pointers, moving the software stack pointer and handling variables kept on the stack. ADDULNK and SUBULNK are the FSR2 forms of ADDFSR and SUBFSR that return after running. The extension is off by default and is turned on with the XINST configuration bit.

An argument that serves as an index or offset is written in square brackets; the assembler flags an unbracketed index. With the extension enabled, brackets also mark index arguments in byte- and bit-oriented instructions. Optional arguments are written in braces.

ADDFSR and SUBFSR add or subtract a 6-bit literal to or from FSR0, FSR1 or FSR2. ADDULNK and SUBULNK do the same on FSR2 only (f = 3) and then return through the TOS, taking two cycles with a NOP in the second. CALLW pushes PC + 2, loads PCL from W and PCH and PCU from PCLATH and PCLATU; unlike CALL it cannot save W, Status or BSR. MOVSF moves the register at FSR2 plus a 7-bit offset to any 12-bit address; MOVSS moves between two FSR2-relative registers. Both reach the whole 4096-byte data space, cannot write PCL, TOSU, TOSH or TOSL, and read 00h if the source resolves to an indirect addressing register; MOVSS runs as a NOP if its destination resolves to one. PUSHL writes an 8-bit literal at FSR2 and then decrements FSR2, pushing a value onto a software stack.

operation.topic: Indexed Literal Offset mode for standard instructions
operation.text: Enabling the extension also turns on Indexed Literal Offset Addressing, which changes how many standard instructions behave and can make legacy code fail. With the extension off, an address in the opcode is a literal location in the Access Bank (a = 0) or in the BSR bank (a = 1). With it on and a = 0, a file argument of 5Fh or less is an offset from FSR2 instead; this touches every byte- and bit-oriented instruction, close to half the core set. With FSR2 = 00h the Access RAM falls back to its normal mapping, which helps backward-compatible code; FSR2 must then be saved and restored across C and assembly routines to keep the stack pointer.

With the extension on, f in byte- and bit-oriented instructions is replaced by a literal offset k, only when f is 5Fh or less, and it must be bracketed. Leaving out the brackets, or bracketing a value above 5Fh, is an assembler error. A bracketed index implies a = 0; giving a explicitly is also an error. The d argument works as before. The assembler needs the extension turned on with the /y command line option or the PE directive.

The extension mainly helps code that uses a software stack. Legacy assembly that addresses Access Bank registers below 5Fh can read or write the wrong locations once those addresses become FSR2 offsets. Large re-entrant C applications gain from it; legacy applications that lean on the Access Bank mostly do not.

MPLAB IDE sets XINST to 0 by default, which disables the extended set and Indexed Literal Offset Addressing. Code built for the extension needs XINST set at programming time, and the language tools must have the extension enabled: through a project setting, a command line option or a source directive, depending on the tool.
When VDD falls through the trip point VHLVD, hardware sets HLVDIF. The flag stays set while VDD is below the trip point and firmware can clear it once VDD has risen back above it.

Every timing figure holds over the standard operating conditions, with VDD in the ranges of the supply voltage and memory programming tables, unless a row says otherwise. Outputs are measured with load condition 1 (RL = 464 Ω to VDD/2 with CL = 50 pF to VSS) or load condition 2 (CL = 50 pF to VSS). CL = 50 pF applies to all pins except OSC2/CLKO, and includes PORTD and PORTE outputs used as ports.

OSC1 high and low times (parameter 3) and rise and fall times (4) are measured on the clock input; the clock period (1) runs between like edges, and the instruction cycle (2) spans four oscillator periods, Q1 to Q4, seen as one period of CLKO.

After the internal POR the Power-up Timer (parameter 33) and then the oscillator start-up time-out (32) run before the internal Reset releases; MCLR held low for at least parameter 30 also resets the device, and I/O pins go high-impedance within parameter 34 of MCLR low or a Watchdog Reset. A brown-out is flagged when VDD stays below BVDD for at least parameter 35. When the internal reference is enabled it needs parameter 36 to settle; the band gap VBGAP is 1.2 V.

In SPI timing, parameter 70 runs from SS falling to the first SCK edge; 71 and 72 are SCK high and low times; 73 and 74 are SDI setup and hold about the sampling SCK edge; 75 and 76 are SDO rise and fall; 78 and 79 are SCK rise and fall in master mode; 80 is SDO valid after an SCK edge; 81 (master, CKE = 1) is SDO setup before the first SCK edge; 77 is SDO going high-impedance after SS rises; 82 (slave, CKE = 1) is SDO valid after SS falls; 83 is SS rising after the last SCK edge.

Start and Stop timing: parameter 90 is SDA setup before the Start (relevant for a Repeated Start), 91 the hold after it before the first clock, 92 SCL high before the Stop and 93 the Stop hold. Data timing: 100 and 101 are SCL high and low times, 102 and 103 SDA and SCL rise and fall times, 106 and 107 data hold and setup about SCL, 109 output valid after the clock and 110 bus free time between a Stop and the next Start.

Setting GO (BSF ADCON0, GO) ends sampling after a short RC delay of about 100 ns typical; the same delay cuts the hold capacitor off the analog input. The ten bits are then resolved one per TAD, from bit 9 down to bit 0 (parameter 131 for the whole conversion). At the end ADRES takes the new result, GO clears to DONE and ADIF is set, and sampling resumes. With the RC clock source selected, the A/D clock starts one TCY later, leaving time to execute a SLEEP instruction.
